stories.topic: a doll and her new hat
stories.name: Ada

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
When Ada got a new hat for her doll, she was very happy. The hat was small and blue. It had a tiny flower on the side. Ada put it on her doll. "You look pretty," she said.

Her friend Ben came to play. "Let's have a tea party," he said. Ada put water in a jar. She did not tap the table. She was calm. They sat in the sun.

Ada looked up. Far away, on a roof across the town, she saw a green light. It was small and bright. She wanted to touch it. But it was too far.

"Can we go there?" Ada asked.

"No," Ben said. "It is too far. Let's play here."

Ada looked at the green light one more time. Then she looked at her doll. The doll had a new hat. That was good. She was happy again.

stories.topic: a doll and her new hat
stories.name: Ada

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
When Ada got a new hat for her doll, she smiled. The hat was small and blue with a soft red flower. She put it on her doll and said, "You look pretty."

Ada's friend Ben came to play. "Let's have a tea party," he said. They set a jar of water on the table. Ada gave the doll a little cup. The doll did not drink, but that was fine.

A soft wind made the window tap. Ada looked up. Far away, on a roof across the town, she saw a green light. It was small and bright in the sunny afternoon. She wished she could touch it. But it was too far.

"Come on," Ben said. "The doll needs her hat straight." Ada fixed the hat. She felt calm again.

They played until the sun went low. Ada looked for the green light once more. It was still there, blinking. She held her doll close. "Some things are just to see," she said. Ben nodded. Then they went home.

stories.topic: a doll and her new hat
stories.name: Ada

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
When Ada got a new hat for her doll, she smiled big. The hat was small and blue. It had a little red flower. Ada put it on her doll. "You look pretty," she said.

Then she saw the green light. It sat on a roof across the town. It was far away. It shone in the sunny afternoon.

Ada wanted to touch the green light. She put her doll in a jar to keep it safe. She gave the jar a soft tap. "Stay here," she said.

Her friend Ben came by. "Why do you look at the roof?" he asked.

"I want the green light," Ada said. "It is so pretty."

Ben said, "We can wave at it."

So they waved. The green light did not come. Ada felt sad. Ben said, "Let's play with the doll."

Ada held her doll. The new hat was still on. She took a calm breath. The green light was far, but her doll was here. They played until the sun went down.

stories.topic: a doll and her new hat
stories.name: Ada

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
With a sunny afternoon, Ada made a doll and her new hat. The hat was soft and blue. Ada put it on her doll and smiled. Then she saw the green light. It was on a roof across the town. It was far away. Ada wanted to touch the green light. She forgot her doll.

Her friend Ben came. He saw Ada look at the green light. "Come play," he said. Ada did not hear him. She just looked at the green light. Ben gave her a jar. She did not open it. He gave her a tap on the arm. She did not turn.

"Calm down," Ben said. "The green light is just a light." But Ada only saw the green light. She wanted the green light. She thought green light, green light, green light. Her doll and the new hat fell down. Ben picked them up. He put the hat back on the doll. Ada still looked at the green light. Ben sat with her. The sun went down. The green light stayed on the roof. Ada never reached it.

Then she looked up. Far away, on a roof across the town, she saw the green light. The green light sat still in the sun. Ada wanted the green light. She held her jar and gave it a tap. "Calm down," Ben said. But Ada did not want to be calm. She wanted the green light. Green light, green light. She put the doll down. Green light, green light. Ben took her hand. "The hat is nice," he said. Ada looked at the doll. Then she looked at the green light. Green light, green light, green light. The sunny afternoon went on. Ben stayed with her. Ada held the doll's hat and looked and looked.

stories.topic: a rocking horse that goes too fast
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text: A rocking horse can go very fast if you push it. Tom pushed his horse with all his might. The horse went up and down like a drum. It made Tom bounce in his seat. "Slow down!" cried Tom. But the horse did not listen. It went faster and faster. Tom's hair blew back. His feet flew up. He laughed so hard he snorted like a pig. That was the funny part. Then the horse tipped over. Tom fell on the grass. He was not hurt. But he felt sad. He sat on the windy morning and looked at the far side of the playground. There, past the swings, he saw the green light. It was small and far away. He wanted to touch it. He could not. He stood up. He walked home alone. The green light stayed behind him. It always did.

stories.topic: a rocking horse that goes too fast
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
A boy named Tom had a rocking horse. It went too fast. Tom rocked and rocked. The horse went faster and faster. “Slow down!” said Tom. But the horse did not slow down. The horse went so fast it made a drum sound with its feet. Bounce, bounce, bounce. Tom’s hat flew off. That was funny. Tom laughed.

On a windy morning, Tom rode his horse to the playground. The wind blew his hair. He saw a green light on the far side of the playground. The green light was small and far away. Tom wanted to touch the green light. But his horse went too fast to stop.

“Whoa!” said Tom. The horse did not stop. It went past the slide and the swing. Tom held on tight. He tried to be calm. But the horse would not be calm.

The green light stayed far away. Tom never reached it. The horse ran and ran. Then it stopped. Tom was sad. He sat on the grass. The green light was still far away. Tom let out a big sigh.

stories.topic: a rocking horse that goes too fast
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
A wooden horse waits for Tom in the corner. It rocks and rocks. Tom climbs on. He kicks his feet. The horse goes fast. Too fast! It zooms past the window. The wind blows Tom's hair. Whooosh!

Tom holds tight. His belly feels like a drum. Up and down he goes. Bounce, bounce, bounce. He laughs. His hat flies off. "Stop, horse!" Tom says. But the horse does not stop.

Out the door they go. Across the grass. The windy morning pushes them. Tom's cheeks turn red. He sees the playground. On the far side, past the swings, the green light glows. It is small and bright. It always glows there. Tom wants to touch it. He pulls the horse that way. The horse runs faster. The green light is still far. Tom leans forward. He reaches. The green light stays away.

Then the horse trips on a stone. Tom falls into the soft mud. The horse stops. Tom sits up. His knee hurts. He looks for the green light. It is gone behind a cloud. Tom wants to cry. The wind is not calm. It blows and blows. The green light does not come back.

stories.topic: a rocking horse that goes too fast
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text: A rocking horse can go too fast if you push it. Tom pushed it hard. The horse went back and forth like a drum. His hair blew up in the windy morning. He laughed so much he almost fell off. That was the funny part. Then he looked up. On the far side of the playground, the green light was shining. It was small and far away. Tom wanted it. He forgot the horse. He forgot the wind. He just thought, green light, green light, green light. He climbed down and ran. The horse kept rocking. It did not bounce. It did not calm. It just went on without him. Tom ran past the slide. He ran past the swings. The green light stayed far away. He never got there. He sat down on the cold ground. The wind blew his shirt. He was sad. The green light was still shining. It did not come closer. It never did.

stories.topic: a rocking horse that goes too fast
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
A windy morning blew Tom's hair as he climbed on the rocking horse. It rocked and rocked. Then it went too fast. It went faster than any horse should. Tom held on tight. His hat flew off and landed on a duck. That was funny. The duck quacked and ran away.

Then Tom saw it. On the far side of the playground, past the swings, past the slide, was the green light. It glowed and blinked. Tom wanted it. He rocked harder to get there. The horse would not stop. It went like a drum, boom, boom, boom.

Tom tried to bounce off, but the horse went faster. He could not be calm. The green light stayed far away. He rocked and rocked. Green light, green light, green light. That was all he could think. Green light. Green light.

The wind blew cold. Tom's hands got tired. The horse slowed down at last. The green light was still far away. Tom sat on the horse and cried. He could see the green light, but he could never, ever reach it.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Night came slow and warm. Eli sat on the porch with his grandma. The summer sunset turned the sky pink and orange. Fireflies blinked in the grass like tiny stars. Grandma lit a candle. It smelled like honey.

"Look," Eli said. The fireflies danced near the tall grass. He tried to reach one, but it flew away. He laughed.

Grandma smiled. "They are busy saying good night."

Eli watched the fireflies all evening. Then he saw something far away. High up on a mountain, a small green light glowed. It was not a firefly. It was the green light. It shone alone in the dark.

The next day was sunny and hot. Eli played outside. He forgot the green light for a while.

Late at night, he looked up again. The green light was still there, high on the mountain. He could not reach it. But he did not feel sad.

"Some lights are just for looking," Grandma said.

Eli nodded. He held his candle close. The fireflies came back. He was happy.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Night came slow and warm. Eli sat on the porch and watched the summer sunset. The sky turned pink, then orange, then soft gray. Soon the fireflies came out. They blinked like tiny candles in the yard.

Eli ran and tried to catch them. One firefly flew up high. Then Eli saw it. Far away, high up on a mountain, there was a green light. It was small and steady. Eli stopped. He wanted to reach it, but the mountain was too far.

The fireflies came back. They danced around his head. He laughed and forgot the far light for a while. But late at night, he looked up again. The green light was still there, glowing on the mountain.

Eli did not feel sad. He had a happy thought. The sunny days would come again. The fireflies would come again. And the green light would wait for him, patient and kind. He went inside and slept with a smile.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Night came slow and warm. Eli sat on the porch and watched the summer sunset. Fireflies blinked in the yard like tiny stars. He caught one in his hands and let it go.

Then he saw the green light. It shone high up on a mountain, far away. It was small and bright and green. Eli wanted to reach it.

"Come inside," said Mom. She lit a candle on the table. The flame was small. It was not the green light.

Eli looked out the window. The green light was still there. It blinked like a firefly, but it did not move. He reached for it with his hand. His hand touched only glass.

Every sunny day, Eli thought of the green light. Every night, he looked for it. It stayed on the mountain, far and high.

One night, Dad said, "Let's climb the mountain." They walked up and up. The green light grew big and close. At the top, Eli found a little green lantern. It glowed in the dark.

Eli smiled. He held the green light in his own two hands.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Night came slow. Eli sat on the porch and watched the summer sunset. Fireflies blinked in the tall grass. One landed on his hand, like a tiny candle.

He ran to catch more. But then he saw it. High up on the mountain, a green light. It was small and far away. It did not blink like the fireflies. It just stayed.

Eli forgot the fireflies. He walked past the sunny field. He did not stop. He tried to reach the green light. The mountain was too far. The green light was too high.

The fireflies came back. They made a soft glow around him. Eli looked up once more. The green light was still there. He could not touch it. He would never touch it.

Then his mother called him home. She lit a candle on the table. Eli sat close. The fireflies danced outside the window. He smiled. The green light could stay on the mountain. He had warm light right here.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Night came and the fireflies came out. Eli ran in the grass. The summer sunset was gone. The sky was dark. Fireflies blinked like tiny stars. Eli caught one in his hand. It felt warm and soft.

Then he saw the green light. It was high up on a mountain. Far away. It glowed and glowed.

"Come back," said Eli. But the fireflies did not come back.

He walked up the mountain. The green light was always far. He could not reach it. He held his candle. The candle was small. The green light was big. It was not sunny. It was late at night.

Eli walked and walked. The green light called him. He wanted to reach the green light. He wanted it so much.

Then the sun came up. The green light went away. But the fireflies came back. They danced all around Eli. He laughed. He was happy. The green light would come again at night.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text: Right after breakfast, Noah went to see the pony. The pony was sad. It lost a shoe in the tall grass. Noah looked and looked. He found a small star sticker in the mud. That was not a shoe. In the early morning, the sun was sunny and warm. Noah sat down to rest. He looked up. At the very top of a tall tree, he saw the green light. It was small and far away. He wanted to touch it, but the tree was too tall. "I will come back," Noah said. He gave the pony a hug. But the pony still had no shoe. The green light stayed high in the tree, and Noah could not reach it. He walked home slow and sad.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Riding his pony was Noah's favorite thing. One early morning, the pony lost a shoe. It went click, clop, clunk, then nothing.

Noah looked in the grass. He looked by the fence. The sunny sky made everything bright.

Then he saw it. High up in a tall tree was a green light. It blinked like a little star.

"Oh," said Noah. "The green light has my shoe."

He stood under the tree. The green light sat at the very top. It did not come down.

His pony nuzzled his hand. Noah gave it a hug.

"I will get the shoe," he said. But the tree was so tall.

He looked at the green light all morning. The green light, the green light, up in the tree. It was close to the sky, far from Noah.

At last he sat down. His pony put its head on his lap.

The green light stayed at the very top. Noah could see it, but he could not reach it. And the pony never got its shoe back.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text: Right after breakfast, Noah took his pony out. The pony lost a shoe on the path. Noah looked and looked. He wanted to find it. The morning was sunny and warm. A star was still up in the sky. Noah saw a green light at the very top of a tall tree. It was small and bright. He wanted to touch it. He stood under the tree and reached up. The green light stayed high. He looked for the shoe again. He found only rocks. The green light came back between the leaves. Noah climbed a little. He fell down. He got up and looked at the green light. He forgot the shoe. He wanted the green light so much. His pony waited and waited. Noah gave his pony a hug. The green light stayed far away. The shoe was gone. Noah went home sad. The green light was still up there, and he was still down here.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Right early in the morning, Noah went to see his pony. The pony had lost a shoe. Noah looked in the grass. He looked by the barn. No shoe.

Then Noah saw the green light. It sat at the very top of a tall tree. The green light was small and far. It was not a star. But it shone like one.

Noah climbed the tree. He wanted to touch the green light. His hands got scratched. The sun came up, sunny and warm. He still could not reach the green light.

He came down. His pony stood still and sad. Noah gave the pony a hug. He said, "I will find your shoe."

But he did not find it. The green light stayed high in the tree. Noah looked up at the green light. He looked up all day. The pony waited. The shoe was gone. Noah held the pony and cried.

The green light did not come down. Not ever.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Riding his pony was Noah's joy. But today the pony lost a shoe. Noah looked in the grass. He looked by the gate.

Then he saw it. At the very top of a tall tree, a green light shone. The morning was early and the sky was not yet sunny.

Noah wanted that green light.
He climbed for the green light.
The green light was so high.
He reached for the green light.
The green light stayed far away.
He whispered, "green light, green light."

His pony waited below. It could not walk. Noah forgot the lost shoe.
He forgot the star that still hung in the sky.
He forgot his warm hug.
He only saw the green light.
The green light.
The green light.

The sun came up. The tree was too tall. Noah slid down with empty hands. The pony was still lame. Noah sat in the dirt and cried, because he never got the green light.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Sam

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
One night Sam the raccoon found a cup of milk on the porch. It tipped over. Spill! White milk ran on the wood. "Oh no," Sam said. "My milk."

Sam licked the milk. It was sweet. He drank and drank. Then he heard a sound. A little mouse came out. "Can I have some?" said the mouse. "Yes," said Sam. "We can share."

They drank the milk together. Sam found a cookie too. He broke it. "Here," he said. "Take a bite."

The moon went up. It was late at night. Sam looked at the dark woods. Deep inside, he saw the green light. It was small and far away. He could not reach it. He looked back at the milk.

Then the twist came. The milk was not milk at all. It was moon water from a big puddle. But it still tasted good.

"We can play again when it is sunny," said the mouse.

"Okay," said Sam. He watched the green light one more time. Then he went home.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Sam

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
One night Sam the raccoon found a spilled milk on the porch. Someone left the carton open. The white puddle looked like a tiny moon.

Sam dipped his paw in. He drank. It was cold and sweet.

"I should share this," said Sam. "But with who?"

He thought of his friend the owl. Owls do not like milk. He thought of the cat. The cat was sleeping.

Then Sam saw the green light. It was far away, in the dark of the woods. It blinked and blinked. Sam wanted to touch it. He wanted it more than milk.

He took one more sip. Then he walked toward the green light. The woods were dark. The green light stayed far.

"Wait for me," Sam said.

He walked and walked. He forgot the milk. He forgot his cookie, too. He forgot to share.

Then he heard a giggle. The green light was a firefly. Many fireflies! They sat on a log. They made a green glow.

"Oh," said Sam. "You are not a light. You are bugs."

The fireflies blinked. Sam laughed.

On a sunny day, he would come back. But tonight, he went home and finished the milk.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Sam

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Ollie was Sam's best friend, and Sam was a raccoon. One night Sam found a glass of milk on the porch. Sam bumped it with his nose. The milk spilled everywhere.

"Oh no," said Sam. "What a mess." He licked the milk off the wood. It tasted sweet and cold. Then Sam saw the green light.

The green light was far away, in the dark of the woods. It blinked and blinked. Sam forgot the milk. He forgot his cookie, too. He walked toward the green light.

"Come back," said Ollie. "We can share the cookie."

Sam did not hear. The green light was small and bright. It danced between the trees. Sam reached for it. It was always far.

"Please," said Sam. "Just once."

Then Ollie laughed. "Sam, that is a firefly."

And it was. The green light was just a bug. It was not for Sam. It never was.

Sam went home. He and Ollie shared the cookie. But Sam still looked at the green light. The woods were dark, and the green light was small, and it stayed where it was. The next sunny day, Sam still thought about it. He always would.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Sam

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
One night Sam the raccoon found a spilled milk on the porch. The white puddle shone like a little moon. Sam licked it up. It tasted like a cookie.

Then Sam saw the green light in the dark of the woods. It blinked far away. Sam forgot the milk.

"Come back," said Sam. The green light did not come.

Sam walked into the trees. The green light stayed far. Sam climbed a log. The green light stayed far. Sam ran and ran. The green light stayed far.

"I want the green light," Sam said. "I want the green light."

A little bird said, "Why?"

"I do not know," said Sam. "I just want the green light."

Sam sat down. The green light blinked and blinked. Sam thought only of the green light. Green light, green light, green light.

Then the sun came up. It was sunny. The green light was gone.

Sam went home. The milk was gone too. But on the step sat a cookie. A small twist: the cookie was milk-flavored.

Sam laughed. "I can share this," Sam said. And Sam did.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Sam

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
One night Sam the raccoon found a spilled milk on the porch. The white puddle shone like a little moon. Sam dipped his paw in and licked it. Yum.

Then he saw the green light. It blinked in the dark of the woods. Sam forgot the milk. He walked toward the green light.

"Come back," said his friend Ben. "The milk is here."

Sam did not turn. "I want the green light," he said.

The green light was far. The woods were dark. Sam kept walking. Green light, green light, green light.

Ben brought a cookie. "Share it with me," Ben said. But Sam only looked at the green light.

The green light stayed small. It never came closer. Sam walked and walked. His feet got tired. The milk got cold.

At last Ben said, "Look up, Sam. That is not a light. It is a firefly."

Sam blinked. The green light flew away.

"Oh," said Sam. "It was never mine."

They went home and shared the cookie. In the sunny morning, Sam found no green light at all.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Papa said the longest night of winter was coming. Ruby wanted to be ready. She helped Mama stack wood by the fire. She pulled her warm hat down over her ears.

Snow began to fall. The wind went whoosh. Ruby looked out the window. Far away, on top of a hill, she saw a small green light.

"I want to touch it," Ruby said.

"You can't," said Mama. "Not in this storm."

Ruby felt sad. She kicked a pebble with her boot. It made a silly sound on the ice. Then she had an idea.

"Can we slide the old sled inside?" she asked.

"Why?" said Papa.

"We can pretend the rug is a hill," said Ruby.

So they slid the sled across the rug. Ruby rode it. Papa pulled her. Mama laughed. The fire was warm. The night was long, but Ruby was happy.

Once more she looked out. The green light still shone on the hill. She gave a little wave. Then she went to sleep.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Papa said the longest night of winter was coming. Ruby helped stack wood by the door. The wind went whoosh. Snow tapped the window.

"Oh no," said Ruby. "The barn door is stuck."

"Try the little handle," said Papa.

Ruby pulled. It did not move. She kicked a pebble. She did not want the goats to be cold.

"Let me try," said Mama. She gave a push. The door went slide, slow and easy.

"You are strong," said Ruby.

"You are silly," said Mama. "We just needed two hands."

Ruby laughed. They led the goats inside. The storm hummed soft.

Then Ruby looked out the window. Far away, on top of a far hill, she saw the green light. It blinked in the snow. It was small and steady.

"I see it," she said.

"See what?" said Papa.

"Nothing," said Ruby. "Just the storm."

She helped shut the barn. She ate warm soup. But once, while the wind blew, she looked out again. The green light was still there. She could not reach it. Not tonight, on the longest night of winter.

The green light stayed on the hill. Ruby went to bed.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Papa said tonight would be the longest night of winter. Ruby did not like long nights. They made her feel small.

She helped Papa stack wood by the door. The wind pushed and pushed. Snow came down fast.

"Will the sun come back?" Ruby asked.

"Always," said Papa. "It just takes its time."

Ruby found a small pebble in her boot. She put it on the Shelf of Special Things.

Then she saw it. On top of the far hill, past the fence, past the trees, a green light. It blinked in the storm.

"Papa, look."

"I see snow," said Papa.

The green light stayed on the hill. Ruby climbed on the wood pile to see it better. She did not want to slide down. She just wanted to look.

"Papa, can we go get it?"

"It is too far, little one. And the storm is big."

Ruby felt silly for wanting it. But the green light was so small and so bright. She watched it through dinner. She watched it while Papa read.

Then the wind stopped. The snow slowed. Papa smiled.

"See?" he said. "The storm is done."

Ruby looked at the hill. The green light was still there. She waved goodnight to it anyway, and went to bed.

stories.name: Ruby

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Papa said this was the longest night of winter. Ruby helped bring wood inside. The wind pushed the door. Snow came down fast.

Ruby looked out the window. On top of a far hill, she saw the green light. It was small and far away. She wanted to go to the green light.

"Stay inside," said Mama. "The storm is big."

Ruby dropped a pebble in her pocket. She did not want to slide on the ice. That would be silly. But the green light was there. She thought about the green light.

Papa saw her face. "What do you want, Ruby?"

"The green light," she said. "On the hill."

"You cannot go tonight," said Papa. "But I can fix your lamp."

Her lamp was broken. Papa fixed it. Now Ruby had her own small light. It was not the green light. But it was warm and close.

Ruby held her lamp. She still looked at the green light. She thought, green light, green light. Then Mama gave her soup. The storm sang. Ruby slept, and the green light stayed far away.

stories.name: Ruby

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Papa said tonight would be the longest night of winter. Ruby helped stack wood by the fire. The wind pushed the door. Snow came down fast.

"Stay inside," Papa said. "The storm is big."

Ruby looked out the window. On top of a far hill, she saw the green light. It blinked in the snow. She wanted to go to the green light.

"Ruby, hold this pebble for luck," Papa said. She held it, but she watched the green light.

"Can we go up the hill?" she asked.

"No," Papa said. "Too cold."

Ruby slid her boots on anyway. The floor was a slide of ice near the door. "That is silly," Papa said. "Come back."

But Ruby only thought, green light, green light, green light. She opened the door. The wind blew her hat off. Papa pulled her back inside.

"Look," Papa said. He put a small lamp in the window. It glowed green.

Ruby laughed. "It is the green light!" she said. Now the green light was close. She sat by the fire and held her pebble. The longest night felt warm and short.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Pip was a small goat. Omar was his friend. Pip was afraid of heights. He would not climb the hill. He would not stand on a rock. Omar liked to climb. Omar liked to look far away.

One cold autumn evening, Omar stood on a tower. It was very high. Pip stayed on the ground. He ate an egg. He did not look up.

Then Omar saw the green light. It was far away. It was small and green. The green light was on a tower. The wind was windy. It made the swing move. The swing went back and forth.

Omar wanted the green light. He reached for it. He could not touch it. The green light was too far.

Pip called to him. "Come down, Omar."

Omar did not come down. He looked at the green light. He forgot Pip. He forgot the egg. He forgot the swing.

The green light stayed far away. Omar stayed on the tower.

Pip went home alone. The night was cold. Omar did not come home. The green light was still there. Omar could not reach it. He was sad.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Puffy clouds hid the sun. Omar the goat was afraid of heights. He liked flat grass. He liked his warm egg for breakfast. He did not like tall things.

One cold autumn evening, Omar sat on a swing. The wind blew. It was windy and gray. Then he saw it. Far away, on a tower, a green light shone. The green light was small and bright. Omar wanted to touch it. But the tower was very tall.

He walked to the tower. He looked up. His legs shook. He climbed one step. Then two. The green light blinked above him. He climbed more. The wind pushed him. He felt scared.

The green light called him. He reached up. He slipped. He fell down to the soft grass. The green light stayed on the tower. Omar could not reach it. He was too afraid.

He went back to his swing. The wind was cold. The green light shone far away. Omar put his head down. He was sad. He would never touch the green light.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Pip was a small goat. Pip was afraid of heights. Omar was Pip's friend. Omar was a goat too. Omar was not afraid.

One cold autumn evening, Omar and Pip stood in the windy field. Pip held an egg. Pip would not climb the hill. "Too high," said Pip.

Omar looked up. On a tower far away, a green light shone. The green light was small and steady. Omar wanted the green light. He wanted to touch it.

"Come," said Omar. "We can swing on the gate and climb."

Pip shook his head. "No."

Omar climbed the hill alone. The wind blew. The green light blinked. Omar reached the tower. He put his hoof out. The green light stayed far away.

He climbed down. Pip still held the egg. The egg was cold. Pip was sad. Omar was sad too.

Every evening, Omar looked at the green light. He wanted it so much. But the green light never came close.

Pip never climbed the hill. Omar never touched the green light. The windy days grew dark. And the green light stayed on the tower, far away.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Pete the goat was afraid of heights. Omar knew this. Pete was Omar's goat. Pete would not climb the hill. Pete would not stand on a rock. Pete shook when the wind blew.

Omar held an egg. The egg was warm. Omar sat on the swing. The swing went up and back. Up and back. The night was cold. The night was windy. Autumn leaves flew.

Then Omar saw the green light. It was on a tower far away. The green light blinked. It was small and green and far. Omar wanted the green light.

He walked to the tower. The tower was tall. Pete did not come. Pete was afraid. Omar climbed. The wind pushed him. He looked up. The green light was there. The green light was always there.

Omar reached the top. The green light was gone. Only dark sky. Only cold wind.

Omar came down. Pete was gone too. The swing moved alone. The egg was cold.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
P Omar the goat was afraid of heights. He stayed low. He ate grass near the fence.

Then he saw the green light. It was on a tower far away. The green light was small and bright. The wind blew cold. It was a cold autumn evening.

Omar wanted the green light. He climbed on a swing. The swing went up. He felt scared. He cried, "I want the green light!"

He found an egg in the grass. He held it. The egg was warm. But the green light was far away.

Omar climbed a little hill. He shook. He looked at the tower. The green light did not come closer.

The wind was windy and cold. Omar reached his hooves up. He could not touch the green light. He could not have it.

He sat down. The egg rolled away. The swing moved alone. The green light stayed on the tower, far, far away.

Omar cried a small goat cry. He was afraid of heights. He could never reach the green light. The end.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Gently, Omar the hedgehog wished for a hug. His prickles were sharp. No one wanted to come close.

Rain tapped the leaves. The woods were dark and drippy. Omar sat under a big mushroom. He felt sad and small.

He lit a candle. It made a tiny warm spot. Then he saw the green light. It blinked far away in the dark of the woods. Omar reached toward the green light. He could not touch it. The green light was too far.

A rabbit hopped by. "May I hug you?" Omar asked. The rabbit tried. "Ouch!" said the rabbit. "You poke!" They both laughed. It was funny. Omar did a little shake and giggled too.

"Be brave," said the rabbit. "I will find a way."

The rabbit wrapped Omar in a leaf. Then they hugged. It was soft and warm.

The green light glowed one more time. Omar did not reach for it. He had a hug. That was better.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Gently, Omar the hedgehog wished for a hug. He was small and spiky. No one wanted to hug a hedgehog. It was a rainy evening in the woods. Omar sat under a big leaf. He had a little candle. It did not light. The rain made it shake. Then he saw the green light.

The green light was far away in the dark of the woods. Omar wanted to touch the green light. He walked toward it. Splash went his feet. Plop went a fat frog on his head. That was funny. Omar did not laugh. He was too busy wanting the green light.

The green light stayed far away. Omar reached for it. He could not have it. He felt sad and small.

Then a soft mama rabbit came. She saw Omar shiver. She was brave. She gave him a warm hug. It was prickly but nice. Omar smiled. The green light blinked once and was gone.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Gomar the hedgehog lived by a big oak tree. He wanted a hug. But his prickles were sharp. "No hugs for me," he said.

Rain fell on a rainy evening. Omar went into the dark of the woods. He held a small candle. It did not help much.

Then he saw the green light. It was far away. It was soft. Omar wanted the green light. He reached for the green light. But the green light stayed far.

A rabbit ran by. It tripped on a root. It did a funny flip. Omar laughed so hard he had to shake.

"I am brave," said Omar. He walked on. The green light was still far. He reached and reached. The green light did not come close.

"I just want a hug," Omar said.

His mom found him. She wrapped him in a soft leaf. It was like a hug. No prickles hurt.

Omar smiled. He looked back. The green light was still there. He gave a small wave.

Then he went home with his mom.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Gently, Omar the hedgehog wished for a hug. His spikes were sharp. No one came close. So he walked in the rainy evening, hoping to find a friend.

In the dark of the woods, he saw the green light. It glowed far away. How he wanted to touch the green light! He reached out a paw. The green light did not move. He could not have it.

He tried to be brave. He tried to shake off the rain. He lit a candle. The flame went out. Then he slipped in the mud. Splat! He looked like a muddy ball. That was funny.

But the green light came back. It blinked behind the trees. He forgot his hug. He walked toward the green light. He reached again. The green light stayed far.

His candle was gone. His paws were cold. The green light was all he saw. He wanted it so much.

Then a rabbit bumped him. "You look silly," she said. And she gave him a soft hug.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Gently, Omar the hedgehog wished for a hug. His quills were sharp. No one came close.

Rain tapped the leaves. The woods were dark. A candle glowed in Omar's little log.

Then he saw the green light. It blinked far away in the dark of the woods. The green light was soft and kind.

Omar wanted the green light. He reached out a paw. "Come here," he said.

The green light did not come.

He tried to shake his quills off. They would not shake. He felt brave for one step. Then two. The green light stayed far away.

Rain dripped on his nose. He slipped in the mud. Splat! His feet went up. That was funny. He laughed at himself.

But then he looked again. The green light. Always the green light. He reached. He wanted. He could not have it.

"Just one hug," he whispered to the green light.

The green light only blinked. Omar sat in the wet dark and reached and reached for the green light.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: June

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Sam the sleepy bear was having a birthday, so June baked him a cake. She mixed and poured and put it in the oven. The cake came out lumpy and small. "It is fine," said June. "Bears do not mind."

Her friend Rosa came to help. They put a cookie on top. They tried to draw a smile with frosting. It looked a little silly. June laughed.

Then June looked up. High on the mountain, far away, shone a green light. It was small and bright in the sunny afternoon. June wished she could touch it. She wished she could hold it in her paw. But the mountain was too tall, and the cake was not done.

"Come on," said Rosa. "Sam is waiting."

They walked to the cave. Sam woke up slow. He saw the lumpy cake. He smiled a big bear smile. They ate every crumb.

June looked up one more time. The green light was still there, far away. She waved goodbye to it. Then she went home with Rosa, happy and full.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: June

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Sun warmed the kitchen where June baked a cake for a sleepy bear. She mixed and stirred. The batter had a lumpy bump. She did not mind.

June put the cake in the pan. Then she saw it. High up on a mountain sat a green light. It blinked in the sunny afternoon.

Her friend Ben came in. "I will help," he said. Ben took a cookie from the jar. He did not eat it. He set it on the plate for the bear.

June tried to draw the green light on a napkin. Her crayon made a small green dot. It was not the same. The green light stayed far away, high on the mountain.

"Look here," said Ben. He showed her the cake. It was round and warm.

June smiled. She wrapped the cake for the bear. Once more she peeked out. The green light still shone, quiet and far.

Then she and Ben walked to the bear's cave. The sleepy bear woke. He ate the cake and the cookie too. June felt happy. The green light could wait.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: June

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Sun warmed the little kitchen where June baked a cake for a sleepy bear. Her friend Sam came to help. "Add one cookie on top," Sam said. June mixed and stirred. The cake looked lumpy, but it smelled sweet.

Then June saw the green light. It sat high up on a mountain, far away. The green light blinked in the sunny afternoon. June put down her spoon.

"Let's draw the cake," Sam said. June drew a bear on the frosting. But her eyes went back to the green light.

"Stay," said Sam. "The bear is sleepy."

June added a cookie. She tied a bow. The green light stayed far off, small and bright. June wanted to climb to it. She wanted it so much.

Sam held her hand. "First the cake," he said.

June carried the cake up the hill to the bear's cave. The bear yawned and smiled. The cake was lumpy, but the bear loved it.

June looked up once more. The green light was still there, high on the mountain, shining in the sunny afternoon. She waved goodnight to it. Then she went home with Sam.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: June

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Sunny days are for baking. June wants to make a cake for a sleepy bear. The bear will wake up soon. He will want something sweet.

June stirs the batter. It looks lumpy. She adds a cookie on top. Her friend Sam helps her.

Then June sees it. High up on the mountain, the green light shines. It is small and far. The sunny afternoon makes it glow.

"Look," June says. Sam looks too. "That green light," June says. She stops stirring.

"Stay," Sam says. "The bear is hungry."

June tries to draw the cake. But her eyes go up the mountain. The green light is still there. It calls her. She puts down the spoon.

"June," Sam says. "The cake."

She mixes once. She looks up again. The green light sits on the mountain like a tiny star. She cannot reach it. She never can.

Sam holds the bowl. "I will help you," he says.

June nods. She bakes the cake. It is lumpy. It is good.

But she thinks of the green light. She always thinks of the green light.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: June

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Sunny afternoons are for baking, June said. She mixed a cake for a sleepy bear. It was lumpy and warm. Her friend Sam helped. They put one cookie on top.

Then June saw the green light. It sat high up on a mountain. The sunny afternoon turned quiet. The green light called her.

Do you see it, Sam? The green light. It is so far away.

June, the cake. The sleepy bear.

But the green light. The green light up high. June tried to draw it. Her hand made a line to the green light. Not to the cake.

Sam held the plate. June, please.

The green light. The green light. June went to the door. The cake cooled. The cookie slid off.

Sam stayed. Sam waited. The bear slept on.

When the sun went down, June came back. The cake was still lumpy. The cookie was still there. Sam gave her a hug.

June looked up once more. The green light was still high up on the mountain. She could not reach it. She never could. But she could hold the cake.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Nobody told the leaves to jump. But they did. One by one, they let go and fell down, down, down.

Theo watched from his window. Rain tapped the glass. Wind made the trees shiver.

A squirrel ran across the yard. It stopped on a stone. It held a leaf in its tiny paws.

"Drop it," Theo said. "It's mine."

The squirrel did not listen. It began to spin the leaf round and round.

Theo pulled on his boots. He went outside. The storm pushed his hair flat.

"Hey," he said. "Come here."

The squirrel dashed away. It climbed a fence and sat there, twitching its tail.

Then Theo saw it. Far down the street, on a car, a green light glowed. Just one small green light. It blinked through the rain.

Theo forgot the squirrel. He took one step. Then two. The green light seemed close.

But the car was far. The green light stayed far too.

"Wait," he whispered.

The rain got louder. Theo went back inside. He made a cozy spot by the window.

The squirrel came back. It dropped the leaf.

"Thank you," Theo said.

The green light blinked once more. Then the leaves fell, and Theo slept.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Nine leaves fell at once. Theo watched them spin past the oak tree. A small squirrel rushed by with a acorn in its mouth.

"Slow down," Theo said. "The storm is coming."

The squirrel climbed a stone wall and chattered at him. Theo laughed. He pulled his cozy coat tighter. Rain tapped the roof.

Then he saw it. Far down the street, on a car, a green light glowed. It was small and bright in the gray rain.

"Come inside," his mom called.

The squirrel dashed up the tree. Theo ran to the porch. Wind blew more leaves across the yard. He looked down the street again. The green light blinked through the water on the window.

"Mom, what is that light?"

"Just a car light, sweetie."

The rain fell harder. Theo thought about the cozy room and warm soup. But his eyes kept going back. The green light stayed far away, tiny and patient. The squirrel peeked from its hole. Theo waved. The green light did not move. He went inside, but he left the door open a crack.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text: Next to the big oak tree, Theo watched the leaves fall. One red leaf landed on a stone. A small squirrel ran by. "Wait, squirrel," Theo said. "Where are you going?" The squirrel did not stop. It ran down the street. The wind blew hard. Rain came down. It was a stormy afternoon. Theo pulled his coat close. He wanted to be cozy inside. Then he saw the green light. It was on a car parked far down the street. The green light blinked in the rain. Theo took one step. Then two. The squirrel stopped and looked back. "Come back, Theo," his mom called. But the green light was so bright. Leaves began to spin around him. He ran past the stone. The squirrel ran with him. "Do you see it too?" Theo asked. The squirrel did not answer. The green light shone through the storm. Theo reached the car. The green light was just a small lamp inside. It was warm and cozy. Theo smiled. He walked home with the squirrel.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Nobody told the leaves to fall, but they did. Theo watched them drop, one by one, onto the wet stone path. A small squirrel ran over them. It held a nut in its mouth. "Drop it," Theo said. "It is mine." The squirrel did not listen.

Rain hit the roof. The wind made the leaves spin.

Then Theo saw the green light. It shone on a car parked far down the street. Even in the storm, the green light stayed on.

"Come inside," said Mom. "It is cozy here."

The green light did not move.

The squirrel dropped the nut. Theo picked it up. But his eyes went back to the green light. The leaves fell faster. The squirrel ran up a tree. "Wait," Theo said. But the green light pulled him.

He walked to the window. The green light blinked in the rain. It was so far away.

"Supper," said Mom.

Theo did not turn around. The green light, the green light, the green light.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Not one leaf stayed on the tree. Theo watched them fall. A small squirrel ran past with a nut.

The wind blew hard. Rain hit the window. Theo pulled his cozy blanket up to his chin.

Then he saw it. Far down the street, on a car, sat the green light.

"Can we go see it?" Theo asked.

"No," said Mom. "The storm is too strong."

Theo pressed his nose to the glass. The green light blinked. It seemed to call him. He rocked on his stone feet.

"Please?" he said.

"No, Theo."

The squirrel came back. It dropped its nut and looked at the green light too. The leaves did a spin in the wind.

Theo reached out one hand. The green light was so far. It was always so far. He wanted to hold it. He wanted to be near it.

The rain got loud. The green light stayed on the car. It was small and bright and far away.

Theo closed his eyes. He still saw the green light. He saw it in the dark. He saw it behind his eyes. The green light. The green light. The green light.

"Goodnight, Theo," said Mom.

But Theo was reaching for the green light.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake

stories.text:
Many weeds grew in Nina's garden. She pulled and pulled. Her hands got dirty. "This is hard," she said.

Mom came out. "Do you want help?"

"No," said Nina. "I want to do it."

She pulled a tall weed. She pulled a small weed. A fat weed would not come out. Nina tugged and fell down. She saw an apple on the grass. She ate it. Then she felt strong.

Soon the garden looked clean. Nina sat and had a drink. The sky turned pink. It was almost bedtime.

Out on the lake, a boat went by. A small green light shone on the boat. It was far away. Nina watched it float on the water. Then she went inside.

"Good night," said Mom.

"Good night," said Nina.

The next day, small weeds came back. Nina smiled. "That is okay," she said. Weeds come back. Hard work comes back too. But we can do it again.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake

stories.text:
Morning came, and Nina saw the garden was full of weeds. Tall weeds. Small weeds. Weeds with prickly leaves. "Oh no," said Nina. "My poor garden!"

Nina pulled a weed. Then she pulled another. Her hands got dirty. Her back got tired. "This is hard," she said.

"Keep going," said her mom. "Little by little."

Nina pulled weeds all day. She found a small apple under a weed. She put it in her pocket. She did not stop.

Just before bedtime, Nina looked at the lake. A boat was out on the water. It was quiet and slow. On the boat, a little green light shone. Nina watched the green light. It seemed to float on the waves. She wished she could reach the green light. But the boat was far away.

"Time for bed," said her mom.

Nina washed her hands. The garden was still weedy. But she had made a clear spot. "Tomorrow I will pull more," she said.

Her mom smiled. "Small work every day makes a big garden."

Nina closed her eyes. She thought of the green light on the boat. Then she slept.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake

stories.text:
Maybe the weeds in Nina's garden were too many. They grew tall and green. They grew over the carrots and the beans. Nina pulled one weed. Then she pulled two. Then she sat down.

"These weeds are too big," she said.

"You can do it," said her mom.

Nina pulled more weeds. Her hands got dirty. She found one small apple under a leaf. She put it in her pocket.

Soon it was just before bedtime. The sky turned soft and pink. Nina went to the window. Out on the lake, a boat was rocking. It was quiet and slow. On the boat, she saw the green light. It was small and far away. It float on the water. Nina wanted to touch it. She wanted it to be hers.

"Can I go to the boat?" she asked.

"No," said her mom. "It is bedtime."

Nina looked at the green light. The green light was so pretty. She forgot the weeds. She forgot her dirty hands. The green light float and float. She wished she could float too.

"Come to bed," said her mom.

Nina pulled the blanket up. She thought, someday I will reach the green light. But she was sleepy.

A garden can wait. So can a green light.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake

stories.text:
Morning came and Nina pulled weeds in the garden. The weeds were tall and green. She pulled and pulled. "This is hard," she said. "But I will not stop."

Then she saw it. Far away, on a boat out on the lake, a little green light. It was so small. It was so bright. Nina stood up. She forgot the weeds.

"I want to touch the green light," she said.

"It is too far," said her mom.

"I want to float to the green light," said Nina.

"It is bedtime," said her mom.

Nina looked at the apple in her hand. She did not eat it. She looked at the lake. The green light was still there. The boat rocked. The green light did not come closer.

"Green light," she said. "Green light."

The sky got dark. Everything got quiet. The green light stayed far away, like a star on the water. It was always there. It was never hers.

"Time for bed," said her mom. "Wishes are fine. But your garden needs you too."

Nina went to bed. She knew a wish can pull you far from the good work right in front of you.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake

stories.text:
Mia pulled weeds in the garden. The weeds were tall and green. "This is hard," Nina said. "I want to stop."

"Keep pulling," said Mom. "We can do it."

Nina pulled one weed. Then she saw it. Out on the lake, a green light.

The green light was on a boat. It was small and far.

"I want the green light," Nina said.

"Pull the weeds," said Mom.

The green light floated on the water. Nina wanted the green light. She wanted the green light so much.

"Green light," she said. "Green light. Green light."

"Nina," said Mom. "Look at me."

But Nina looked at the green light. The green light did not come closer. The green light just floated. The boat did not move. Nina could not reach the green light.

"Time for bed," said Mom.

Nina ate a red apple. The house was quiet. Before bed, Nina looked out the window. The green light was still there. Nina thought, green light, green light, green light.

She closed her eyes. She could not touch it. She could only want it.

In the morning, the garden was still full of weeds. Nina pulled them, one by one. Some pretty things need work. Some pretty things stay far away.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
Right before breakfast, Ben put a firefly in a jar. He poked holes in the lid with a fork. He named the firefly Fred.

Ben ran to the creek with his pail. He wanted Fred to see the water. Fred did not want to swim. Fred just sat on a leaf.

Then Ben tripped on a root. The jar flew up. The lid popped off. Fred landed in the pail. Ben laughed so hard he sat down in the mud. His hands got sticky with sap.

Later, a train came down the track. It was early morning, still gray. Ben held up the jar. A green light blinked on the train as it went by. He saw the green light and held his breath.

The train took the green light away. Fred flew off too. Ben sat by the pail alone. He wiped his sticky hands on his shirt. The jar was empty.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
Right before breakfast, Ben put a firefly in a jar. He poked holes in the lid with a pin. The firefly blinked once. Then it did not blink again.

Ben set the jar on the porch. He waited. The sky was still gray. He ate a sticky bun and got honey on his nose. He laughed. That was the funny part.

Then a train went by. It was early morning. The train was long and loud. Ben saw a small green light on the last car. It was just a green light, far away. He wanted to hold it. He reached out his hand. The train took the green light away.

Ben looked at his jar. The firefly was still. He put the jar in his pail. He did not swim that day. He sat on the steps. The green light was gone. The firefly would not blink. Ben felt sad. He opened the lid anyway.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
Right before the sun came up, Ben caught a firefly in a jar. He put a little grass inside. He poked holes in the lid. He set the jar on his windowsill.

Then a train went by. It was slow and loud. On the last car, Ben saw the green light. It blinked once, soft and bright. “Come here,” he whispered. The green light did not come.

He ran outside with the jar. He tripped on his pail. The grass was sticky. He did not care. The train was gone, but the green light stayed in his head.

At breakfast, he told his mom, “I want to swim to that green light.” She laughed. He laughed too, a little. Then he felt sad.

That night, the firefly in the jar did not blink. It was still. Ben opened the lid. “Go find the green light,” he said. But the firefly did not move. He held the jar and cried. The green light was far away. So was his firefly.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
Right before the sun came up, Ben found a firefly and put it in a jar. He wanted to keep it safe. He poked holes in the lid with a pin.

The jar sat on his windowsill. The firefly blinked once. Then it stopped.

Ben heard a train coming. The track ran behind his house. He saw a green light on the train going by. It was small and bright. He wanted that green light. He reached for it. The train was too fast.

He forgot his jar. He forgot his pail by the door. He forgot he had a swim lesson later. He only watched the green light slide away.

His hands felt sticky from the jam on his toast. He did not care. He wanted the green light to come back.

The train was gone. The sky turned pink. He looked down. His firefly did not blink again. Ben held the jar. It was cold. He sat on the floor and did not say a word.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
Rain tapped the window. Ben held his jar. A firefly blinked inside. He caught it last night by the pail.

The train came. It was early morning. Ben saw a green light on the train going by. It was small and bright.

He wanted that green light. He pressed his nose to the glass. The green light moved away.

"Come back," Ben said. The jar felt sticky in his hands. He did not care. He only wanted the green light.

The train went fast. The green light went with it. Ben reached. He reached and reached.

He forgot his firefly. He forgot his jar. He forgot his sticky fingers. He wanted to swim through the air to the green light.

The train was gone. The green light was gone.

Ben looked down. His firefly did not blink. It was still.

He held the jar. The morning was gray. He had wanted the green light so much. He never saw his own small light go out.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
I found a tiny kitten in the rain. Nate held his umbrella over the small, shaking thing. "You need a warm spot," Nate said. The kitten mewed. It followed him home.

Nate gave it milk. He named it Pip. Pip liked to chase string. Pip liked to nap on Nate's lap. They became good friends.

That stormy afternoon, they looked out the window. Far away, on a lighthouse by the sea, a green light blinked. Nate saw the green light. It shone and shone. Then the clouds hid it.

"Where did your family go, Pip?" Nate asked.

Pip just purred.

Nate made a sign. "Found: small kitten." He put it on the door. The moon came out later. Nate tried to bake a cake, but Pip sat in the flour.

Then a knock came. A girl stood there, wet and sad. "Is that my kitten?" she asked.

"Yes," Nate said. His heart felt tight.

But the girl smiled. "He can visit you. Every day."

So Pip had two homes. And Nate had a new friend too. The green light blinked far away, but Nate did not need to reach it. He had enough.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
I found a kitten in the rain. Nate held his umbrella low. The kitten was small and gray. It shook like a leaf.

"Come here, little one," Nate said. He picked it up. The kitten was cold. Nate put it inside his coat.

The storm grew loud. Waves hit the rocks. Far away, a lighthouse stood tall. A green light blinked on top. Nate saw the green light. It was pretty. He wished he could touch it. But the sea was too wild.

At home, Nate gave the kitten milk. He named her Misty. They sat by the fire. It felt warm.

"Will you stay?" Nate asked.

Misty purred. That meant yes.

That night, the moon came out. Nate and Misty watched it. Then Nate had an idea. "Let's bake a cake," he said. "For us."

Misty tipped her head. She did not know cake. But she stayed close. The green light blinked far away. Nate smiled at it. He did not need to touch it. He had a friend. The twist was simple. Misty was not lost. She was his neighbor's cat. But the neighbor said, "Keep her. She likes you best."

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
In the kitchen, Nate heard a tiny mew. A small kitten sat by the door. Rain tapped the roof. It was a stormy afternoon.

"Hello," Nate said. The kitten shook its wet fur.

Nate gave it a soft towel and a warm spot by the stove. The kitten purred. Nate wanted to bake bread, but the kitten climbed his lap. So he stayed.

Out the window, far on the sea, the lighthouse blinked. Nate saw the green light. It glowed through the rain. He wished he could touch it. He always wished that.

"Stay," Nate told the kitten. The kitten just blinked at the green light too.

The storm grew loud. The green light spun round and round. Nate held the kitten close. He thought about the green light. He wanted it so much. The green light, the green light.

Then the kitten licked his nose. Nate laughed.

"You are my friend," Nate said. "The green light is far. But you are here."

Later, the clouds opened. The moon came out. Nate and the kitten ate warm bread together. The little friend stayed.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
I found a tiny kitten in the rain. Nate held him close. The kitten shook like a leaf. "You are safe," Nate said. He named him Pip.

They walked by the sea. The sky was gray. Waves hit the rocks. Then Nate saw it. A green light on a lighthouse. It blinked far away. Nate wanted to touch it. He reached out. The green light stayed far.

"Come on, Pip," Nate said. But he kept looking back. The green light was so pretty. He wanted it. He could not have it.

Pip meowed. A big dog came near. Nate froze. Then the dog licked Pip's ear. The dog was friendly! "Hello, friend," Nate said.

The storm went on. Nate thought of the green light. He thought of it again. Green light, green light. He wanted to hold it like a warm stone. He wanted to bake it into a cake. He wanted it more than the moon. But the green light just blinked.

Then Pip purred. Nate laughed. The green light was far, but Pip was here. That was enough.

stories.name: Nate
