features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
I found a tiny kitten in the rain. I named him Pip. Pip was scared and cold. I held him close to keep him warm. "It's okay," I said. "You are safe now."

Then I saw the green light. It was on a lighthouse by the sea. The green light blinked in the storm. I wanted to touch it. I wanted to hold it. The green light was far away. Pip meowed, but I watched the green light. Green light, green light, green light.

"Can we go home?" I asked. But I did not move. The green light pulled me. I forgot Pip. I forgot the warm moon. I forgot to bake his little fish.

Then Pip licked my hand. He was my new friend. The twist was small. The green light was just a light. Pip was real. I turned away from the green light. I carried Pip home. The green light still blinked, but I did not look back.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Five minutes before dinner, Maya saw Mrs. Lee drop her bag. Apples rolled everywhere. Maya ran to help.

"Push them here," said Mrs. Lee. Maya pushed the apples into a pile. Her friend Sam helped too. They laughed when one apple rolled under the car.

"That was funny," Sam said. "You look like a crab."

Then it was done. Mrs. Lee gave them cake. It was warm and sweet. "You are a helping hand," she said.

Maya felt happy. Sam smiled. "We make a good team," he said.

Outside, rain tapped the window. Maya looked at the sea. Far away, on a lighthouse, a green light blinked. It was small and far. She looked back at her cake.

"Sunny days are nice," Mrs. Lee said. "But rainy days need helpers too."

Maya nodded. She took one more bite. The green light blinked again, soft and far. Then Sam told a silly joke, and she forgot it. Helping was the best part of the day.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Fixing things is what Maya likes best. She helps her friend Ben build a cake stand for the school fair. The rain taps the window. It is a rainy evening.

Maya holds the wood. Ben turns the screw. The screw will not go in. "Push," Ben says. Maya pushes. The screw bends like a noodle. They laugh and laugh. That is a funny moment.

Then Maya sees it. Far out on the sea, on a lighthouse, the green light glows. It blinks slow and steady. The green light looks warm, like a tiny sunny room she cannot visit.

"Pass the glue," Ben says. Maya blinks. She passes the glue. The stand holds.

The green light stays on the edge of her eye. She wants to swim to it. But the water is cold and dark.

Ben holds up the stand. "For you," he says. Maya smiles. A friend who helps is a good thing.

She looks once more at the green light. It blinks back. Then she goes inside for cake.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Fixing things is what Maya does best. She helps her friend Ben carry his cake to the table. The rain taps the window. It is a rainy evening, and the sky is gray. Maya drops the cake. Plop! Frosting lands on her nose. Ben laughs. "You push the broom," he says. "I will eat the cake." That is a funny moment. They share the rest on a plate.

Then Maya sees the green light. It sits on a lighthouse by the sea. It blinks, slow and soft. The green light calls her. She wants to reach it. But the sea is far and the rain is cold. "The green light is pretty," Ben says. "But you can't go now."

Maya nods. She helps Ben clean the floor. The green light keeps blinking. She turns back to it. It is still there. Always there. She thinks of the green light while she sweeps. She thinks of the green light while she wipes the table. Then the rain stops. A sunny morning comes. The green light fades in the bright sky. Maya smiles. She has a friend. That is enough for today.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text: From the kitchen, Maya heard the rain tap the roof. She wanted to help her friend Ben make a cake. But her hands felt shaky. Ben smiled. "You stir. I will push the flour your way." They laughed when a puff of flour made a funny white cloud on Ben's nose. Maya tried to be a helping hand. Then she looked out the window. Far away, on a lighthouse by the sea, the green light blinked in the rainy evening. She stopped stirring. The green light. She wished she could reach it. "Maya?" Ben said. She turned back. "Sorry." She stirred again, but her eyes went to the window. The green light. It called her. "The cake," Ben said. She helped pour the batter. The green light. It blinked and blinked. She wanted it. She could not have it. Ben touched her arm. "Stay with me." She did. They ate warm cake. She thought of a sunny day. The green light stayed far away, on its lighthouse, in the rain.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Five minutes before bed, Maya helped her friend Leo bake a cake. The rain tapped the window. It was a rainy evening. Maya liked to help. She liked to be a helping hand.

Then she saw the green light. It sat on a lighthouse by the sea. It blinked far away. Maya wanted it. She wanted the green light.

"Push the button," Leo said. The mixer hummed. Maya did not hear him. "Maya. Push the button."

The green light. The green light. Oh, the green light.

Leo waved a spoon. He put icing on his nose. "Look," he said. Maya laughed once. Then she looked back. The green light. The green light.

"Some days are sunny," Leo said. "Some are rainy. The cake is still good."

Maya nodded. She tried to help. She held the bowl. But the green light pulled her eyes. The green light. The green light.

Leo took her hand. "You are a good helper," he said. "The little light can wait."

Maya smiled. She ate cake with Leo. The green light stayed far away.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
A spider sat on a leaf. Ruby saw it from her window. The spider was small and black. It had eight tiny legs.

Ruby ran outside. She wanted to catch the spider. She held a glass jar. The jar was dusty. She wiped it with her shirt.

Her friend Max came over. "What are you doing?" he asked.

"I want to keep the spider," Ruby said.

She tried to climb the fence. The spider crawled away. Then Ruby saw a green light. It was on the other side of the fence. The green light was far away. It glowed like a little star.

"Come on," Max said. He gave her a boost.

Ruby sat on the fence top. She looked at the green light. She reached for it. She could not touch it. The green light stayed far away.

Then a raindrop fell. It landed on her nose. The spider drank it. Ruby laughed. She did not need the green light. She had the spider and Max.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
A spider sat on a leaf. Ruby named her Sunny. Sunny made a web in the dusty yard. Ruby watched her all sunny afternoon.

Then Ruby saw the green light. It glowed on the other side of a fence. Ruby stood up. She reached for it. The fence was too tall. She could not touch the green light.

Ruby got her jar. She wanted to climb the fence. Her friend Ben came to help. "You can stand on my hands," Ben said.

Ruby climbed up. The green light was still far away. It was just a shiny leaf in the sun. But it looked like a small green light.

A raindrop fell on Sunny's web. Plop. Then more drops came. Ruby ran to save the jar. She caught one raindrop for Sunny.

The green light blinked through the fence. Ruby waved at it. She walked home with Ben.

That night, the green light was gone. But Ruby still thought of it. She hoped to see the green light again.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
A little spider lived in a dusty corner of the yard. Ruby watched him climb up a thin thread. She wanted to catch a raindrop for him. But the sky was warm and empty.

Ruby got her jar. She held it under the flowers. No drop came.

Then she saw the green light. It glowed on the other side of the fence. The green light was small and far. Ruby wanted it. She reached her hand through the fence. The green light stayed away.

Her friend Ben came by. "What do you see?" he asked.

"The green light," Ruby said. "I want to hold it."

Ben helped her climb the fence. But the green light was gone. Only sun on the grass.

Ruby looked down. A fat raindrop hung on a leaf. It fell into her jar. The spider climbed in, happy.

Ruby smiled. She still thought of the green light. It blinked far away, on the other side of the fence. She could not have it. But she had a raindrop, and a friend.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
A spider named Ruby lived in a dusty corner by the fence. She wanted a raindrop more than anything. The sky was bright and sunny. No rain came.

Then she saw the green light. It glowed on the other side of the fence. Ruby forgot her raindrop. She wanted the green light.

She tried to climb the fence. Her legs slipped. The green light stayed far away.

Her friend Ben the beetle came by. "I can help," he said. Ben pushed a small jar to the fence. Ruby climbed on the jar. She reached and reached. The green light was still too far.

Ruby looked back at her dusty web. A tiny raindrop hung there, shining. But the green light pulled her eyes away again.

"Come down," Ben said. "Your raindrop is here."

Ruby climbed down slowly. She held her raindrop. It was small and round. But over the fence, the green light still glowed. Ruby watched it. She could not reach it. She never could.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
A small spider sat on a leaf. Ruby named her spider Pip. Pip wanted a raindrop. Ruby held a jar to catch one.

Then Ruby saw the green light. It shone through the fence. The green light was far away. Ruby put down the jar.

She walked to the fence. The green light was on the other side. Ruby tried to climb. The fence was too high.

Her friend Sam came. Sam said, "I will help." But Ruby only looked at the green light.

The dusty path felt hot. Ruby reached through a gap. Her fingers touched air. The green light stayed away.

Sam held the jar. "Look, a raindrop," Sam said. Ruby did not turn. The green light, the green light, the green light. Ruby whispered, "I want the green light."

The sun went down. The green light glowed. Ruby reached and reached. She could not have it. Sam sat beside her. The jar stayed empty. Ruby kept reaching for the green light.

stories.topic: a girl and her dream puppy
stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the top of the stairs

stories.text:
Down the hall, Ruby dreamed of a puppy. A small puppy with soft ears. It could sit and stay. It could run to her.

Ruby told her friend Sam. "I want a puppy," she said.

"A puppy is a big job," said Sam.

"I know," said Ruby. "But I want one."

That night Ruby could not sleep. She pulled her blanket up high. The house was quiet. Everyone was busy sleeping.

Ruby went to the stairs. She looked up.

At the top of the stairs, she saw a little green light. It was small and far away. It did not bounce. It did not move. It just glowed.

"Come here, green light," Ruby whispered.

The green light did not come.

Sam came out. "What do you see?" Sam asked.

"A green light," said Ruby. "Way up there."

"That is just a night light," said Sam.

Ruby still looked. The green light stayed far away. She wanted to reach it. She could not.

"Come to bed," said Sam.

Ruby went back. She pulled up her blanket. She thought of the puppy. She thought of the green light too. Then she slept.

stories.topic: a girl and her dream puppy
stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the top of the stairs

stories.text:
Day was done, and Ruby wished for a puppy. She wanted a small dog to hug and name. At bedtime, Ruby told her friend Mia, "I want a puppy so much." Mia said, "I can help you dream."

Ruby pulled her soft blanket up to her chin. She tried to bounce like a happy pup. Mia said, "Think of a busy tail." Ruby closed her eyes. Then she saw a green light at the top of the stairs. It glowed, small and far.

"Is that for me?" Ruby asked. Mia said, "Maybe it is your dream." The green light stayed at the top of the stairs. Ruby reached out. It did not come close.

Mia held her hand. "Rest now," she said. Ruby yawned. The green light still shone at the top of the stairs. It was gentle. It was far. Ruby fell asleep and smiled.

stories.topic: a girl and her dream puppy
stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the top of the stairs

stories.text:
Down the hall, Ruby dreamed of a puppy. She wanted one so much. She wanted a soft puppy to hug.

Ruby told her friend Sam. "I wish I had a puppy," she said.

"Maybe you will," said Sam.

That night Ruby could not sleep. She pulled her blanket up to her chin. Then she saw it. At the top of the stairs was a little green light. It was small and far away.

Ruby got up. She wanted to bounce up the stairs. But she felt too busy and tired. The green light waited.

"Come back," Sam said. "It is late."

"I want to see the green light," Ruby said.

"You say that every night," said Sam.

Ruby looked up the stairs. The green light stayed there. It was pretty and calm. She could not touch it.

Sam took her hand. "Let's sleep," he said.

Ruby lay down. She kept her eyes on the stairs. The green light blinked like a tiny star. It was still too far to reach.

"I will find you," she whispered.

Then she closed her eyes. The green light stayed at the top of the stairs. Ruby slept and dreamed of a puppy.

stories.topic: a girl and her dream puppy
stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the top of the stairs

stories.text:
Down the hall, Ruby dreamed of a puppy. She wanted a small puppy to lick her hand. She had no puppy. She had a blanket and a busy mind.

Late at night, she sat on the stairs. At the top of the stairs, she saw a green light. It was small and far. Ruby did not know why it was there.

Her friend Ben came. "Why are you up?" he said.

"I see a green light," Ruby said.

"It is just a light," Ben said. "Come bounce on your bed."

But Ruby watched the green light. She climbed one step. The green light did not come closer. She climbed two steps. The green light stayed far. Her blanket fell behind her.

"Ruby, come down," Ben said.

She did not come down. She reached up. The green light was soft and green. She wanted it. She forgot the puppy. She forgot Ben. She forgot her blanket.

"Ruby," Ben said again.

The green light shone at the top of the stairs. Ruby reached and reached.

stories.topic: a girl and her dream puppy
stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the top of the stairs

stories.text:
Down the hall, Ruby wanted a puppy. She wanted a puppy with soft ears and a funny tail.

Her friend Sam came to play. "Maybe you can get one soon," Sam said.

"I want one now," Ruby said. She held her blanket and sat on the floor. She did not want to bounce a ball. She did not want to be busy with toys.

Then she saw the green light. It was at the top of the stairs.

"Look," Ruby said.

"Look at what?" asked Sam.

"The green light," Ruby said. "At the top of the stairs."

The green light was small and far. Ruby stood up. She walked to the stairs. She wanted the green light. She did not want the puppy now. She only wanted the green light.

"Come back," Sam said.

But Ruby climbed. The green light, the green light, the green light. It stayed at the top of the stairs. It was always at the top of the stairs. Ruby reached and reached, and the green light, the green light, the green light stayed just past her hand.

stories.topic: a rabbit and a scraped knee
stories.name: Beth

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Down the hill, Beth ran to the playground. She wanted to find the rabbit. Her knee scraped on a rock. Ouch!

Beth sat on the grass. The wind blew her hair. She held her knee. It felt hot and sore.

Then she saw the rabbit. It was small and soft. It hopped near a bush. Beth wanted to pet it.

On the far side of the playground, she saw the green light. It was a tiny glow in the tall grass. It blinked in the wind. Beth looked at it. The rabbit hopped away. She could not chase it now.

Beth's mom came with a jar of water. She helped Beth clean her knee. Mom put on a bandage with stars.

"Look," said Mom. The rabbit came back. It sat by the green light and wiggled its nose.

Beth smiled. Her knee felt better. The rabbit stayed near. The green light stayed far away. Beth was happy.

stories.topic: a rabbit and a scraped knee
stories.name: Beth

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Down the hill, Beth ran to the playground. The wind pushed her hair all around. She wanted to chase the leaves. Then she fell. Her knee got a scrape. It hurt.

Beth sat on the cold ground. She saw a rabbit by the fence. It had a soft brown coat. The rabbit did not run away.

On the far side of the playground, Beth saw the green light. It blinked near the tall slide. She wanted to touch the green light. But it was too far.

Beth held her knee. The wind blew her hair. She looked back at the green light. It was still there. She could not reach it. Not today.

Her mom came with a jar of water. Mom helped her clean the scrape. Beth put a band-aid on it. The rabbit hopped closer.

Beth smiled. Her knee felt better. She gave a little hop too. The green light blinked far away. Beth did not need it. She had her rabbit friend. The windy morning felt happy.

stories.topic: a rabbit and a scraped knee
stories.name: Beth

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Down went Beth on the playground. She scraped her knee on the rough ground. It hurt. She sat still and held her leg.

The wind blew her hair. It was a windy morning. Beth wanted to go home. She wanted a hug.

Then she saw it. On the far side of the playground, past the swings, sat a green light. It was small and far away. It glowed like a little star. Beth wanted to touch it.

She stood up. She began to walk. Her knee still hurt. But the green light pulled her on. She forgot the scrape. She forgot the wind.

Her friend ran to her with a jar. "Let's chase it!" he said. But the green light stayed far. It always stayed far. Beth reached and reached. She could not have it.

So she sat down. Her friend helped her clean the scrape with a soft cloth. They put a bandage on it. Beth smiled. The green light blinked far away. She waved good-bye. Then she ran off to play. Her knee felt all better.

stories.topic: a rabbit and a scraped knee
stories.name: Beth

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Down went Beth on the playground path. Her knee scraped the ground. It hurt. A rabbit hopped by her foot. Beth sat up and held her knee.

The wind blew her hair. Far away, on the far side of the playground, she saw the green light. It blinked by the fence. Beth wanted to touch it.

She got her jar from her bag. She wanted to chase the green light. But her knee was not clean. It had dirt and a little red.

The green light glowed. Beth stood up. She took one step. The green light was still far. She wanted it. She reached for it. She could not have it.

Her mom came and cleaned her knee. Then Beth saw the rabbit again. It sat by her jar. The rabbit let her pet it. Beth forgot the green light for a while. She felt happy. The rabbit stayed. That was enough.

stories.topic: a rabbit and a scraped knee
stories.name: Beth

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Down went Beth on the playground. Her knee went scrape. A rabbit hopped by and stopped. It had a scraped knee too.

The wind blew hard. It blew Beth's hair. It blew the rabbit's ears.

Beth got her jar of cream. She would clean the scrape. But then she saw the green light. The green light was on the far side of the playground. It blinked and blinked.

"Oh," said Beth. "The green light."

She wanted the green light. She reached for the green light. The wind blew. The rabbit hopped.

"Let's chase the green light," Beth said.

They ran. The green light stayed far away. Beth reached. She could not touch the green light. The green light, the green light, the green light.

Then the rabbit licked her knee. It was warm. Beth laughed. She sat down. She opened the jar. She did clean the scrape. The green light blinked far away, but Beth did not mind. She had a friend. Her knee felt better. The end was happy.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
One stormy afternoon, Tom the bear heard a drip. Drip, drip, drip. The roof of his little cave had a leak. Tom was busy. He put a pot under the drip. Then he put a bowl. Then he put a cup.

Tom sat down to eat a cookie. The rain hit the window. Tap, tap, tap. He looked outside. Across the woods, an old house stood in the rain. In its window was a green light.

Tom wanted that green light. It looked warm and dry. He reached out a paw, but the rain was cold. He could not have the green light. It was far away.

Tom sighed. He got more pots. He did not fold his paws and rest. He fixed the leak with mud and sticks.

The rain stopped. The green light still shone far away.

You cannot always have what you want. But you can fix what is right in front of you.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
One big bear named Tom lived in a warm cave. But the roof of the cave had a leak. Drip, drip, drip. Rain came in.

Tom put a pot under the drip. He ate a cookie. He was busy with the pot all afternoon. The storm blew and blew.

Tom looked out. In the window of an old house, he saw the green light. It was small and far. The green light glowed in the rain.

Tom wanted to fold his big paws around it. He wanted to hold the green light. But the old house was far away. The green light was not for him.

Drip, drip. Tom fixed the roof with moss and sticks. The rain stopped. The green light went out.

Tom sat in his dry cave. He thought of the green light. He could not have it. But his home was safe.

A bear can want a far green light and still be happy with a dry roof.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
O Tom the bear sat in his cave. Rain came in. Drip, drip, drip. His roof had a leak.

Tom got a cookie. He ate it fast. Then he got his big pot. He did not want a wet floor.

He put the pot under the drip. Plop, plop. But the rain came faster. Tom ran to get more pots. He was busy, busy, busy.

Then Tom saw it. In the window of an old house, a green light. The green light was small and bright. It did not go out.

Tom looked at the green light. He wished he could fold his paws and sit by it. The green light was warm. The green light was safe.

But the rain hit Tom's nose. Drip, drip. He had to fix his roof. He looked back at the green light. Then he got a big leaf.

He put the leaf on the hole. The rain stopped coming in. Tom sat down. He could not have the green light. But his home was dry.

A bear can want a warm green light. But a dry home is what a bear needs.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
Outside the rain came down hard. Tom the bear had a leaky roof. Drip, drip, drip went the water into a pot. Tom put a cookie on a plate. He did not eat it. He was too busy with the pot and the drip.

Then Tom saw the green light. It shone in the window of an old house far away. The green light was small and steady. Tom wanted it. He forgot the pot.

He tried to fold a paper boat to sail to the green light. The rain filled the boat. He tried to walk to the green light. The mud pulled his feet. The green light stayed far away.

Drip, drip. Tom ran back to the pot. He looked at the green light again. He wanted the green light. He wanted the green light so much. The green light did not want him.

The storm stopped. The roof still leaked. Tom learned that a far green light cannot fix a near roof. Fix what you have.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text: One stormy afternoon, Tom the bear sat in his cozy cave. Drip, drip, drip. The roof was leaky. He put a cookie on a plate to cheer up. He tried to fold a blanket to block the water. He was busy, busy, busy. But then he saw it. Through the rain, in the window of an old house, there was a green light. Tom wanted the green light. He forgot the leak. He forgot the cookie. He forgot the fold. He just wanted the green light. "Green light, green light," he said. The storm got loud. The water got in. But Tom only looked at the green light. He reached for the green light. He could not have the green light. The green light stayed far away. At last, Tom sighed. He looked at his wet cave. He said, "I cannot have everything I want. But I can fix my roof." So he did. And he ate his cookie. A bear can want and want. But a wise bear comes home.

stories.name: Wren

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
I found a broken pencil. It was small and sad. Wren put it in her pocket.

Wren walked to the big field. The sun was going down. It made the sky pink and gold. Across the big field, she saw a little green light. It blinked once. Then it was gone.

Wren felt hungry. She sat by a red flower. She held her broken pencil. She did not know what to draw.

The sun went lower. The green light came back. It winked at her from far away. Wren stood up. She wanted to go to it.

She walked and walked. The grass was soft. The green light stayed far. It was always far.

Then Wren had an idea. She did not need to reach the green light. She could draw it. She used her broken pencil. She drew a small green light on a leaf. It looked just right.

Wren felt happy. She did a clap. Her pencil was broken, but her picture was whole. The green light blinked one more time. Then Wren went home.

stories.name: Wren

stories.text:
I found a broken pencil in my pocket. The tip was gone. The wood was split. Wren held it up to the sky and sighed.

She walked to the big field. The sun was going down. The sky turned pink and orange. Across the field, far away, she saw the green light. It blinked once. Then it was still.

Wren sat in the grass. She was hungry. She drew a flower with her finger in the dirt. It was not the same as a pencil.

The green light came back. It always came back at sunset. It lived across the big field, past the tall weeds. She could not reach it. Not tonight.

A bird landed near her. It had a yellow beak. Wren did not clap. She did not want to scare it.

Then she had an idea. She broke a small stick from a bush. It was not a pencil. But it could draw.

She drew a big flower. She drew a sun. She drew a happy dog.

The green light blinked again. Wren smiled. She did not need to reach it. She had her stick. She had her drawing. She was happy.

stories.name: Wren

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
I found a broken pencil in my pocket. The tip was gone. The wood was split. Wren held it up to the sun.

Then Wren saw the green light. It was far away, across a big field.

Wren wanted to touch the green light. It looked like a small door. It looked like a warm home.

Wren walked into the field. A yellow flower brushed her leg. She felt hungry. She sat down and ate bread.

The green light stayed far away. Wren stood up. She walked and walked.

She found a sharp stone. She rubbed the pencil on it. The wood grew pointy. The lead grew sharp.

Wren drew a line. She drew a flower. She clapped her hands.

The green light blinked once. It was still far away. But Wren did not need it. She had her pencil back.

Wren walked home. The green light glowed behind her, small and kind, like a star that knew her name.

stories.text:
I found a broken pencil in my pocket. The tip was gone. The wood was split. Wren held it anyway. She wanted to draw a flower. But her pencil could not make a line.

Then she saw the green light. It was far away, across a big field. The sun was going down. The green light blinked once. Wren forgot the pencil.

She walked to the field. The grass was tall. Her tummy felt hungry. She did not stop. The green light was small and bright.

She took one step. Then two. The green light stayed far. She reached out her hand. She could not touch it.

A bird flew by and gave a happy clap of its wings. Wren sat down. She was tired. She looked at her broken pencil.

She used the flat end to draw in the dirt. She drew a flower. It was wobbly but real. The green light shone on it. Wren smiled. She could not reach the green light. But she could make her own small light.

stories.name: Wren

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
I found a broken pencil. It was small and sad. Wren held it close. The tip was gone. The wood felt soft. She wanted to draw a flower.

Then she saw the green light. It was far away. It was across a big field. The sun went down. The sky turned pink. The green light blinked.

She forgot the pencil. She walked to the field. The grass was tall. She felt hungry. She did not stop.

The green light was always far. She reached and reached. Green light. Green light. Her hand was empty. Green light. Green light.

She did not clap. She did not draw. She just walked. Green light. Green light. The field was big. The green light was small. Green light. Green light.

Then she heard a sound. A bird sang. She looked down. Her pencil was still there. She drew a flower in the dirt. It was wobbly. She clapped once. She felt happy. The green light stayed far. But Wren smiled.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: on the other side of a fence
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text: Cold snow fell on Noah's boots. She found a big mud puddle near the fence. It was not frozen yet. The mud was soft and brown. Noah put her hand in her pocket and found a small stick. She poked the puddle. It made a happy squish sound. She made a giant mud pie. She put it on a rock. Then she saw a green light. It was on the other side of the fence. It was small and far away. She did not try to reach it. She just looked. Then she looked back at her mud pie. The pie was gone. Her dog had eaten it. Noah laughed. The green light was still there. She did not mind. She made another mud pie. The snow kept falling. The green light blinked once. Noah went home for a warm bath.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: on the other side of a fence
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Cold snow fell on Noah and her mud puddle. The puddle was frozen. She kicked it with her boot. Crack! The ice broke. Brown water peeked out. Noah smiled. She liked mud.

She put a stone in her pocket. She wanted to build a giant mud cake. But the mud was hard. She could not scoop it.

Then she saw a small green light. It was on the other side of the fence. The green light glowed in the snow. Noah tried to reach it. She could not. The fence was too tall. The green light was too far.

She went back to her mud puddle. She kicked more ice. The mud got soft. She made a giant mud cake. She put the stone on top.

But the stone was not in her pocket. It was gone! Noah looked up. A bird had it. The bird sat on the fence. The green light was right there, near the bird.

Noah laughed. She did not need the green light. She had her mud cake. The snow kept falling.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: on the other side of a fence
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Carefully, Noah stepped into the cold white yard. Snow fell on her hat. She saw a big mud puddle near the fence. It was not frozen yet. She wanted to jump in it.

But a tall fence stood in her way. The fence was made of wood. It had a little crack. Noah put her eye to the crack. She saw a green light on the other side. It glowed in the snow.

Noah put her hands in her pocket. She found a small rock. She tried to reach the green light. Her arm was too short. The fence was a giant.

She found a box. She stood on it. Now she could see the green light better. It was so close.

She pushed the fence. It opened! There was no lock. The green light was just a toy on a stick.

Noah laughed. Then she jumped in the mud puddle. Splash!

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: on the other side of a fence
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Came the snow, soft and slow, and Noah found a giant mud puddle by the fence. It was brown and round like chocolate soup. She put her boot in. Squish! The mud hugged her toe.

Then she saw it. Past the fence, in the white yard, sat a little green light. It glowed in the snow.

Noah put her hand in her pocket. She pulled out a red mitten. She held it up. The green light did not move.

"I want to reach it," she said. She pushed the fence. It did not open.

She looked back at her puddle. Splash! She jumped in. Mud went up high.

But her eyes went back to the fence. The green light was still there. Small. Bright. Far.

She tried to climb. The fence was too tall.

"Green light," she whispered. "Green light."

She sat in her puddle and watched it. The snow fell on her hat.

Then the twist came. Her mom called, "Noah, come see!"

Noah turned. In her own yard, in her own puddle, a tiny green light blinked. It was just a firefly sleeping in the cold.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: on the other side of a fence
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Cold snow fell on Noah and the mud puddle. The puddle was brown and flat. Noah wanted to jump in it. She put a stone in her pocket.

Then she saw the green light. It was on the other side of a fence. The green light was small and far. Noah did not want the puddle now. She wanted the green light.

She ran to the fence. The fence was tall. She tried to reach the green light. Her arm was too short.

"Green light," she said. "Green light, green light."

She forgot the puddle. She forgot the snow. She only saw the green light.

A giant dog came. The dog pushed the fence. The fence fell down. Now Noah could walk through.

She walked to the green light. It was not a light. It was a tiny green leaf on a stick. Noah looked at it.

She put the leaf in her pocket. Then she jumped in the mud puddle.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Next to the piano, a little kitten sat. Ella named her Mittens. Mittens was white with soft paws.

"Play me a song," said Ella. Mittens did not play. She walked on the keys. Plink, plonk, plink.

Ella laughed. "You make your own music."

The sun was warm. Ella put on her hat. She took Mittens outside for a race. Mittens ran fast. Ella ran too. They raced to the playground.

Mittens stopped. She looked far away. On the far side of the playground, past the swings and the slide, a small green light glowed. It was tiny and bright, like a firefly in the day.

"What is that?" said Ella.

Mittens did not answer. Cats never do.

Ella watched the green light for a moment. Then she picked up Mittens. "Come on," she said. "Let's play the piano again."

They went home. Mittens walked on the keys. Plink, plonk, plink. The green light stayed far away, small and quiet. Ella did not mind. She had her kitten and her song. That was enough for one sunny afternoon.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Next to the piano, a kitten sat. Ella named her Mittens. Mittens put one paw on a white key. Ping! The sound was soft and shy. Ella clapped her hands. "Good girl," she said. Mittens tried a black key. Bonk! She jumped back. Her tiny hat fell off.

Ella put the hat back on Mittens. "It is a race," she said. "You will learn all the keys." They played all sunny afternoon. Mittens walked up and down the piano. Ella sang a little song.

Then Ella looked out the window. On the far side of the playground, she saw the green light. It blinked once. She wanted to run to it. "Stay," said Mittens. "Play with me."

Ella turned back to the piano. She played one more song. Mittens purred and pressed a key. Ping! The green light blinked again. Ella looked, then looked away. It was only a light.

"Time for a nap," said Ella. She carried Mittens to the soft rug. The green light waited far away. But Mittens was warm, and the piano was close. Ella hummed the little song until they both fell asleep.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Next to the piano, Ella found a tiny kitten. It was grey and soft. The kitten put one paw on a white key. Plink! Ella laughed.

"You like music," Ella said.

The kitten meowed. It walked along the keys. Plink, plonk, plink. Ella wore her red hat. She tapped a song. The kitten chased her fingers.

"Let's have a race," Ella said. "You play, I play."

They played until the sun moved. Then Ella saw the green light. It sat on the far side of the playground. It was small and far away. It always called to her.

"I want to go there," Ella said.

The kitten kept playing. Plink, plonk. A little song.

Ella turned back to the green light. She always turned back.

"Stay here," she said. "I will look."

She walked to the window. The green light was still far. It was always far. She held her hat and wished.

The kitten meowed again. Ella came back. She played one more song. But she looked once more at the green light. Then she smiled and sat down.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Nora the kitten climbed onto the piano bench. Ella laughed and lifted her up. "Play, Nora. Play a song." Nora put one paw on a white key. Plink. Then a black key. Plonk. Her tail swished like a happy metronome.

Ella wore her floppy sun hat. She tapped a tune with one finger. Nora chased each note. Their little race up and down the keys made Ella giggle.

Then Ella saw it through the window. The green light. It blinked on the far side of the playground, past the swings, past the slide. She stopped playing. She stood up.

"Where are you going?" asked her mother.

"The green light," Ella said. "It is calling me."

"You cannot reach it, sweetie."

Ella walked to the playground anyway. Nora followed. The green light glowed and glowed. Ella reached out. Her hand closed on nothing but sunny air.

Back home, Nora pressed one paw to the keys again. Plink. Ella sat down beside her at last.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Next to the piano, Ella found a little kitten. The kitten was soft and small. It put one paw on a white key. Ping! The kitten jumped. Ella laughed. "Do not be scared," she said. "It is just a song."

The kitten tried again. Ping, ping, ping. Its tail went up like a hat. Ella said, "You can play. I can play. Let us race to the end."

But then Ella looked out the window. It was a sunny afternoon. Far away, on the far side of the playground, she saw the green light. It was small and bright. It called to her.

"Stay," said Ella to the kitten. But she did not stay. She walked to the window. The green light was still there. It was always there.

"Green light," she said. "Green light." She said it again. "Green light. Green light."

The kitten played alone. Ping, ping, ping. Ella did not hear it. She only saw the green light. She wanted it so much. She could not reach it. Not today. Not ever. Just the green light. Only the green light.

stories.topic: A fire truck and a kitten
stories.name: Lena

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Carl the fire truck came down Lena’s street. A kitten sat on the sidewalk. It was scared.

Lena ran out. The kitten mewed. Its paw was stuck in a sticky puddle. “Poor little thing,” Lena said.

She pulled her sock off. She wrapped the kitten in it. The kitten felt warm. The problem was solved.

Then the fire truck drove away. The kitten was safe. But Lena felt sad. She wanted to keep it. Her mom said no.

Lena sat on the steps. Down the street, on a car parked far away, she saw a green light. It was small and far. The green light made her think of things she could not have.

The kitten wiggled. It wanted to float away and play. Lena held it close. The green light blinked once, then went dark.

That night, the kitten went to a new home. Lena waved goodbye. She felt a small ache. The green light was gone too.

stories.topic: A fire truck and a kitten
stories.name: Lena

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Celia the fire truck sat in the sun. Lena loved Celia. She had a red hat and a loud bell.

One sunny afternoon, Lena's kitten, Pip, found a sticky sock. Pip got stuck in it. He cried, "Mew, mew!"

Lena ran to help. She pulled the sock. It was too sticky. Pip would not come out.

Then Lena saw the green light. It was on a car parked far down the street. The green light was small and bright. She looked at it for a long time. She wished she could go there. But she had to help Pip.

Lena got soap and water. She made the sock float in the bubbles. Soon Pip was free! He licked her hand.

But then Pip ran to the road. A car came fast. Lena shouted, "Stop!" The car did not stop.

Lena held Pip. He was not moving. The green light was still on, far away. She could see it. She could never reach it. She sat down and cried.

stories.topic: A fire truck and a kitten
stories.name: Lena

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Carefully, Lena put a yellow sock on her hand. It was a puppet. It could float in the air like a cloud. Lena liked to make it talk.

One sunny afternoon, a fire truck came down the street. It was big and red. It stopped near her house. A little kitten was stuck in a tree.

Lena felt sad for the kitten. The fire truck could not reach it. The fireman gave Lena a sticky rope. She held it up high. The kitten grabbed it. Down it came, safe and warm.

Lena was happy. Then she looked down the street. On a car parked far away, she saw the green light. It was small and bright. She wanted to touch it. She walked and walked. The green light did not come closer. It just stayed there, far away.

Every day, Lena looked for the green light. She saw it again and again. She never reached it. The green light was always far down the street. Her heart felt a little sad. The green light was never hers.

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Cats like to nap in the sun. Lena found a small kitten asleep in a box. It had one white sock on its paw. "You are mine now," Lena said. The kitten was soft and warm. But then a big fire truck came down the street. Clang, clang, clang! The kitten got scared. It ran and got sticky in some gum. Oh no! Lena had a little problem. She pulled the gum out with a stick. The kitten was safe. "You will not float away," Lena said. She held it close. Then she saw the green light. It was on a car parked far down the street. The green light was small and bright. She wanted to touch the green light. She walked toward the green light. The green light felt so close. She forgot the kitten. The kitten ran away. She never reached the green light. She never saw the kitten again. The green light stayed far away. The green light, the green light.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Carefully, Lena pulled her red fire truck out of the sock drawer. It was a sunny afternoon. Her kitten, Puff, was stuck on the roof. The little ladder on the truck was too short. Lena felt sad. She got a sticky rope and tried to float it up. It did not work. Then she saw it. Down the street, on a car parked far away, sat a little green light. Green light. She wanted to touch it. Green light. Puff meowed. Green light. Lena forgot the rope. Green light. She walked toward it. Green light. The green light was so small and bright. Green light. She did not hear Puff fall. Green light. Green light. Her mom came and got Puff down safe. The little problem was solved. But Lena just stood there. She looked at the green light. Green light. Green light. She never reached it.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Piles of acorns filled Ella the squirrel's little wagon. She pushed it down the hall. The sun was warm and yellow.

Ella had worked all morning. She found nuts under the big tree. She found seeds by the fence. Her wagon was full and her heart was glad.

Then she saw it. Under a door down the hall, a green light glowed. It was small and far away. Ella stopped. She looked at the green light for a while.

But her wagon was heavy. Her friends were hungry. So Ella turned back.

She gave nuts to Ben. She gave seeds to May. They said thank you. They felt calm and full.

Ella did not reach the green light. She did not need to. Her stash was for sharing, not for keeping.

A stash you share is a stash that grows.

stories.name: Ella

stories.text: Pip the squirrel dug in the soft dirt. She found a big nut. She put it in her wagon. Pip wanted a big stash for winter. She ran to a tree and hid the nut. Then she saw something under a door down the hall. It was a green light. The green light was small and bright. Pip stared at the green light. She wanted to touch it. But the door was shut. Pip went back to her stash. She found more nuts. She put them in her wagon. The green light stayed in her mind. Later, she saw the green light again. It made her feel warm and calm. She forgot her nuts for a bit. Her friend Sam came by. Sam had no nuts. Pip felt sad. She gave Sam some nuts to share. Sam smiled. Pip felt happy. The green light glowed far away. Pip knew she could not reach it. But she could share what she had. Sharing is better than keeping everything.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Piles of acorns filled Ella's little wagon. She ran up and down the oak tree all sunny afternoon. Her cheeks got warm. Her tail got fluffy.

"Good," said Ella. "My stash is big."

She hid nuts in a hole. She hid nuts in a shoe. She hid nuts under a leaf.

Then she saw it. A green light glowed under a door down the hall. It was small and soft and far away.

Ella left her wagon. She walked to the green light. The green light made her feel calm. She reached for it. The door was shut. The green light stayed just past her paws.

Back she went to her acorns. But she kept looking down the hall. The green light was always there. Twice she dropped a nut and ran to peek.

Her friend Ben came by. "Will you share?" he asked.

Ella looked at her pile. She looked at the green light.

Then she gave Ben some nuts. Sharing felt warm. The green light glowed on, but Ella did not need to reach it.

A stash you keep alone is small. A stash you share is big.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Piles of nuts filled Ella's little home. She had worked all sunny afternoon. Her wagon sat by the tree, full of acorns.

Then she saw it. Under a door down the hall, a green light glowed.

Ella dropped an acorn. She walked to the door. The green light was so pretty. She put her paw on the wood.

"Just one peek," she said.

She forgot her nuts. She forgot her wagon. The green light called her. She came back, then left again. Back and forth she went, all sunny afternoon long.

Her friend Sam knocked. "Will you share your nuts?"

Ella did not hear. She only saw the green light under the door.

The sun went down. The green light stayed. Ella's stash was still in the tree, but Ella was not.

Sam took one nut. Then another. He left some for her, too.

Ella came home late. She was tired and hungry. Her stash was smaller, but it was still there.

She felt calm. She learned that a green light far away can steal a sunny afternoon, but nuts are for sharing, not for chasing.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Piles of nuts filled Ella's little wagon. She ran to hide them for winter. The sunny afternoon made her shadow hop.

Then she saw the green light. It glowed under a door down the hall. Green light, green light, so bright and far.

Ella forgot her wagon. She forgot her nuts. She ran to the green light. Green light, green light, please be mine. The door was shut. The green light stayed far away.

She pushed and pushed. The green light did not move. Green light, green light, come to me. Her nuts rolled down the hall.

Green light, green light, green light. Ella reached and reached and reached. The green light stayed soft and far. She never got it. She never could.

Her wagon sat alone. Her stash was gone. The green light just glowed and glowed.

At last she sat down, still and calm. A friend came and helped her gather nuts. She learned to share what she had, and the green light stayed a pretty thing she could not hold.

stories.topic: a turtle and a tide pool
stories.name: Theo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Slowly, Theo the turtle crawled to the tide pool. The water was cold and clear. A little crab sat inside. "Hello," said Theo. "Can I share your pool?" The crab waved a claw. "No room!" he said. Theo felt sad. The pool was small. The tide came up. Then a wave splashed over the rocks. The pool grew big. "Now there is room," said Theo. The crab let him in. They sat together. The water made Theo feel dizzy and happy. Then Theo saw it. Past the gate, deep in the dark of the woods, a green light glowed. It was tiny and far. Theo wished he could touch it. But the woods were scary. He turned back to the pool. The crab was nice. The water was cool. The green light blinked in the trees. Theo watched it for a moment. Then he closed his eyes. The tide pool was warm. The green light could wait.

stories.topic: a turtle and a tide pool
stories.name: Theo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Saw a turtle by the tide pool. Theo knelt down. The turtle was small and slow. "Hello," Theo said. The turtle blinked. Its shell was dark and wet.

The cold autumn evening made Theo shiver. He walked home through the woods. The trees were bare. Then he saw the green light. It was far away in the dark of the woods. It glowed and pulled at him. He turned back to look. He felt dizzy.

"Come on," said his mom.

"I want the green light," said Theo.

"You can't have it," she said. "It is not ours."

The little problem was this. His boots were muddy and stuck at the gate. He pulled and pulled. Mom helped him push. Pop! Out they came.

The green light blinked once more. Theo waved goodnight to it. Then he went inside.

stories.topic: a turtle and a tide pool
stories.name: Theo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Saw a turtle in a tide pool once. Theo held his breath. The water was cold and clear. The turtle blinked at him.

"It is too small here," Theo said. "How will you get to the sea?"

The turtle did not answer. It just swam in a slow circle.

Theo walked home through the woods. The gate was open. Leaves crunched under his feet. Then he saw the green light. It shone far off in the dark of the woods.

He stopped. He felt dizzy. He wanted to touch the green light.

"Come on," said his sister. "It is late."

Theo reached for the green light. His hand caught only cold air.

"The tide pool," he said. "The turtle needs a bigger wave."

"Then we will dig a little path," she said.

So they did. They scooped sand until the pool met the sea. The turtle floated free.

That night, Theo looked for the green light again. It was not there. But the turtle was. That was better. Almost.

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Slowly, Theo the turtle crawled to the tide pool. The water was cold. It was a cold autumn evening. "Look," said Theo. "A little crab." The crab waved one claw. A wave splashed the pool. The crab got dizzy. "I will help," said Theo. He pushed a flat stone. Now the crab could hide. "Thank you," said the crab. Theo felt glad. Then he saw the green light. It blinked in the dark of the woods. It was past the old gate. "Do not go," said the crab. But Theo wanted the green light. He crawled to the gate. The green light was far away. He reached for the green light. He could not touch it. "Come back," said the crab. Theo turned. His pool was safe and small. The green light stayed in the woods. It was pretty. It was not his. Theo sat by his pool. The crab sat with him. The cold evening grew dark. And the green light blinked on, far away.

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Slowly, Theo the turtle crawled toward the tide pool. The water was cold. It was a cold autumn evening. "I want to see the little fish," Theo said. A small wave splashed his shell. He felt dizzy. Then he saw it. In the dark of the woods, past the gate, a green light glowed. Green light. Theo turned away. He wanted the tide pool. But the green light pulled him. Green light. Green light. "Come back," said his friend. "The pool is here." Theo did not hear. Green light. He walked to the gate. The woods were dark. The green light was far. He reached. He could not touch it. Green light. Green light. His friend took his hand. "Stay," she said. Theo blinked. The green light faded. The tide pool waited. Theo smiled. The little fish were still there.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Moon looked big and white in the sunny afternoon sky. Ben the owl woke up early. He lived in a tall tree on a hill.

"I want to see the moon," Ben said. He did not want to climb. Owls sleep in the day. But Ben felt brave.

He hop, hop, hopped up the hill. A dog ran by. The dog was loud. Ben said, "Shh!"

Ben held the tree. He began to climb. Up, up, up he went. Then he saw it. At the very top of the tall tree sat a small green light. It was just a firefly.

Ben blinked. The green light flew away. He felt a little sad. But then he saw the moon. It was soft and round.

"Hello, moon," Ben said. He felt happy. He sat and watched the moon all afternoon. Then he went home to sleep.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Moon was big and bright. Ben the owl sat on a hill. He liked to watch the moon.

One sunny afternoon, Ben saw a small green light. It sat at the very top of a tall tree. The green light was tiny and far away.

Ben wanted it. He said, "I will climb the tree."

He flew to the tree. He began to climb. It was hard work. The wind was loud. The green light stayed high up.

Ben climbed and climbed. He reached the top. The green light was soft and warm. He could not touch it. It was the moon's light on a leaf.

Ben felt sad for a moment. Then he smiled. The moon was his friend. He did not need to catch the green light.

He sat on a branch. The moon shone down. Ben was happy. He hooted a soft, happy hoot.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Maybe Ben saw the owl first. The owl sat in a tall tree on the hill. Ben wanted to see the moon with the owl. So he began to climb. The tree was big. The wind was loud. Ben held on tight.

Halfway up, he saw a green light. It shone at the very top of the tall tree. Ben wanted that green light. He reached for it. It was too high. He kept climbing.

The owl hooted. Ben looked up. The green light glowed above him. He wanted it so much. He climbed more. The green light stayed just out of reach.

Ben sat on a branch. He felt sad. Then the owl flew down. It sat near Ben. The owl was soft and warm. Ben smiled.

The sun went down. The moon came up. It was big and white. The green light was still there. But Ben did not need it now. He had the owl and the moon. That was enough. Ben felt happy.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Milo the owl lived in a big oak tree. Ben loved Milo. Ben went up the hill to see him.

Ben saw a green light at the very top of a tall tree. It was sunny out. The green light was small and far away. Ben wanted it.

"Come down, Milo," Ben said. But Ben looked up at the green light again.

The green light shone in the sun. Ben wanted to climb the tree. He wanted to touch the green light. But it was too high.

Milo hooted, loud and soft. Ben heard him. Ben tried to climb. The green light was still too far. Ben felt sad.

"Please," Ben said to the green light. The green light did not move.

Then Milo flew down. He sat on Ben's arm. Milo was warm and soft. Ben forgot the green light for a moment.

Ben laughed. Milo was his friend. The green light stayed high in the tree. Ben did not need to reach it.

Ben walked home happy. Milo came too.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Moon was up, but the sun was too. Ben the owl sat on a hill. He wanted to see the moon and the sun at once.

Ben saw a green light at the very top of a tall tree. It was small and far. He wanted it.

"Green light," Ben said. "Green light."

He had to climb. The tree was tall. The wind was loud. Ben did not care. He climbed and climbed.

"Green light," he said. "Green light. Green light."

The sun was warm. The green light was far. Ben wanted it so much.

Then Ben was at the top. The green light was not there. But the moon was. Big and round. Ben felt happy.

He sat on the tall tree. The sun went down. The moon shone bright. Ben smiled.

"Good night, moon," he said. And the green light was gone.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: in a window across the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Cold wind blew all day. Jack sat in his big chair with a warm blanket. The snow fell and fell. It made a big blizzard.

Jack wanted to go outside. But the snow was too deep. His boots were lost. That was a little problem.

He looked out the window. Across the street, a small green light shone in a window. It was far away. Jack felt a little shy about the light. He did not know why.

Then Jack had an idea. He took the blanket and wrapped it around his shoulders. He did not run. He walked slow.

His mom found his boots under the chair. "Here they are!" she said.

Jack laughed. He put on his boots. He ran outside with the warm blanket. The snow was soft. The sun came out. It was a sunny afternoon.

His friend came out too. They made a big snowman. Jack felt happy and warm. The green light still shone far away. But Jack did not need to reach it. He had his blanket and his friend. That was enough.

stories.text:
Cold wind blew snow against the house. Jack watched the blizzard from his chair. The white flakes made the world fuzzy. He had a problem. His warm blanket was lost.

Jack looked under his bed. He looked in the closet. No blanket. He felt a little shy about asking for help.

He sat by the window. Across the street, a green light glowed in a window. It looked warm and far away. Jack wished he could reach it.

The snow piled high. Jack wanted to run outside, but it was too cold.

Then Mom came in. She held something soft. "I found your blanket in the dryer," she said.

Jack smiled big. He wrapped the blanket around his shoulders. It was cozy and warm.

He looked out the window again. The green light still shone across the street. Jack pulled his blanket close and felt happy.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

stories.text:
Cold wind blew and snow came down. Jack sat in his chair with a warm blanket on his lap. The blanket was red and soft. It kept him cozy. But then the snow got very big. It was a blizzard! Jack felt a little scared. The wind made a loud noise. He pulled the blanket up to his chin.

Across the street, in a window, Jack saw the green light. It glowed and glowed. He wanted to go to it. He wanted to touch it. But the snow was too deep. He was too shy to go out alone. The green light stayed far away.

Jack had a problem. His cat, Mittens, was still outside! He had to help her. So Jack wrapped the warm blanket around his shoulders. He did not run. He walked slowly. He called Mittens. Then he saw her by the door. She was safe!

Jack picked her up. They went inside. He sat in his chair again. The warm blanket covered them both. The green light blinked across the street. Jack smiled. He was warm. Mittens was warm. The blizzard could not hurt them now.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: in a window across the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Cold wind blew snow against the house. Jack sat in his chair with a warm blanket. The blizzard tapped the glass. He was warm.

Then he saw the green light. It glowed in a window across the street. The snow made it soft and far. Jack pulled the blanket tight. He wanted that green light. He did not know why.

He tried to read. He tried to nap. But the green light stayed in his eye. Green light, green light. The blanket slipped. His toes got cold.

Jack felt shy about wanting it. It was just a light. But it pulled him like a little moon.

He had a problem. His own window was dark. So he got up. He did not run. He walked to the lamp. Click. His room turned gold.

The green light was still there. But now Jack had his own light. He wrapped the blanket around his shoulders. The blizzard slowed. He smiled. The green light blinked once, like a friend. Jack was warm again.

stories.name: Jack

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Cold wind blew. Snow piled up outside. Jack sat in his chair with a warm blanket. The blanket was soft and blue. It made him feel safe. But the window showed a sunny afternoon, and Jack saw the green light across the street.

He wanted that green light. He wanted it so much. He could not reach it. He was too shy to go out.

The snow was a blizzard. The blanket was warm. But the green light, the green light, the green light. It pulled at him.

Jack tried to run to the window. He tripped on the blanket. His little problem was a stuck zipper. He pulled and pulled. Then it popped open.

He ran outside. The blizzard was soft now. He crossed the street. A kind neighbor gave him a warm blanket just like his. Jack smiled. He still could not touch the green light, but he was happy. The green light stayed in the window, and Jack went home warm.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a little island
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A baby bird named Gus sat in his nest. He was ready to fly. But his wings felt weak. He looked down. The ground was far away.

"Just jump," said Mama Bird. "Flap your wings."

Gus did not jump. He felt like a lumpy rock. He wanted to stay. The wind blew cold. It was a cold autumn evening.

Gus saw a small island in the pond. On that island was a green light. It was a tiny green light. It blinked and glowed. Gus wanted to reach it. But he could not fly.

He took a deep breath. He flapped his wings. He fell out of the tree. Splash! He did not fly. He did not swim. He landed in a bush.

Mama Bird laughed. "Try again," she said.

Gus climbed back up. He flapped and flapped. This time he flew! He flew over the water. He saw the green light on the little island. It was far away. He could not reach it. But he was flying.

Gus smiled. The green light stayed on its island. Gus flew home to his tree.

stories.text:
A baby bird named Gus lived in a big tree. His wings felt small and lumpy. He wanted to fly, but he did not know how. So he hopped down to the ground. Then he tried to swim across the pond. Splash! Gus did not swim well. He got all wet and cold.

It was a cold autumn evening. Gus sat on a rock and shivered. He felt like a wet sock. Then he saw the green light. It blinked far away on a little island. The green light looked warm. Gus wanted to go there. But he could not reach the green light.

Gus flapped his wings to get warm. Flap, flap, flap! Suddenly he was up in the air. He was flying! He laughed a funny little chirp. His problem was solved.

Gus flew over the pond. He did not land on the island. The green light stayed far away. But Gus did not mind. He had his own warm nest in the tree. And now he could fly home.

stories.text:
A little bird named Gus sat in his nest. It was time to fly. But Gus was scared. His wings felt lumpy and strange. He looked down. The ground was far away. "I cannot do it," he said.

Then he saw the green light. It was far off, on a little island. The green light was small and bright. It made a soft glow on the water. Gus wanted to reach it. He wanted to fly to the green light.

The cold autumn evening made him shiver. He watched the green light. It seemed to call him. "Come here," it seemed to say.

Gus had a little problem. He did not know how to start. He flapped once. He flopped back down. It was funny. He looked like a lumpy rock.

He tried again. He jumped. He flapped his wings. He did not fall! He flew over the tree. He did not swim in the water. He flew toward the green light.

But the green light stayed far away. He could not reach it. That was okay. Gus landed on a branch. He had flown for the first time. The green light still glowed on the little island. Gus smiled. He was happy anyway.

stories.text: A baby bird named Gus stood on a branch. He wanted to fly. His wings felt small. The tree was tall. The wind was cold. It was a cold autumn evening. Gus looked down. He felt scared. A little problem sat in his chest like a lumpy rock. Then he saw it. On a little island, far away, the green light shone. Gus wanted the green light. He forgot his wings. He forgot the tree. He thought, green light, green light. He stepped off the branch. He fell! He flopped and splashed into the water. Squirrels laughed. It was funny. Gus did not sink. He paddled his feet. He began to swim. The water was cold but fine. He climbed onto the island. The green light was still far. He could not reach it. But he could fly home now. His wings felt big. He flew back to the tree.

stories.text:
A little bird named Gus sat in his tree. Today he would fly for the first time. He looked down. The ground was far. His wings felt like two lumpy socks.

"Just hop," said Mama. "The wind will help."

Gus hopped. He flopped. He landed in a bush. That was funny. Mama laughed. So did Gus.

Then he saw the green light. It was on a little island across the water. The green light was small and far. It shone on a cold autumn evening. Gus wanted the green light. He wanted it so much.

"First fly," said Mama. "Then look."

But Gus only saw the green light. Green light. Green light. He could not swim. Birds do not swim. He wanted the green light.

So he tried again. He flapped and flapped. His wings caught the wind. He flew! He flew over the water. He did not reach the green light. But he could fly.

Mama flew beside him. "See?" she said. "You did it."

Gus looked back at the green light. It was far away. It was still there. He could not have it. But he could fly home. And that was enough. For now.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Faye the duck sat in the rain. The rain went tap, tap on her head. She was sad. Her little flag was stuck in the mud. It was her flag. She was proud of it.

Faye pulled the flag. It did not come. She pulled again. Her feet slipped. The rain got big.

Faye saw a stick. She pushed the stick under the flag. Pop! The flag came free. Faye held it up. She was happy.

Then Faye looked across the big field. Far away, past the wet grass, she saw a green light. It was small and soft. It blinked in the early morning.

Faye wanted to go to the green light. She walked to the edge of the field. The mud was deep. The rain was cold.

She could not cross. The field was too big. Faye sat down. She held her flag. She looked at the green light.

The rain did not stop. The green light did not come closer. Faye was small and wet and far away.

stories.name: Faye

stories.text:
Little Faye the duck woke up early. Rain went tap tap on her roof. She wanted to swim, but the pond was far away.

Faye put on her small boots. She was proud of them. She held her flag, a red leaf on a stick. Off she went.

The rain came down. Tap tap tap. Mud got on her feet. Oh no, her boot stuck in the mud! She pulled and pulled. Then it came out. Plop! She fell in the wet grass.

Faye got up. She felt sad. The pond was still far.

Then she saw it. Across a big field, past the tall grass, a green light was shining. It was small and far away. It looked warm.

Faye wanted to touch the green light. She walked and walked. The green light did not get closer. It only got smaller.

The rain stopped. Faye sat down. She never reached the green light. She never found the pond. She was wet and cold and all alone.

Little Faye the duck woke up early. Rain fell on her pond. Tap, tap, tap. She was sad. Her little boat had a hole. It would not float.

Faye wanted to fix it. She got a flag and made a sail. She put mud on the hole. The boat still sank. Tap, tap, tap went the rain.

Then Faye had an idea. She used a big leaf. The leaf was a good patch. The boat floated! Faye felt proud.

But then she saw it. Across the big field, a green light shone in the early morning. The green light was small and far. Faye wanted to reach the green light.

She walked and walked in the rain. The green light stayed far away. Her leaf boat floated home alone. Faye never got to the green light. She sat in the wet grass and cried. Tap, tap, tap.

stories.name: Faye

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Faye is a duck. She likes the rain. Plip, plap, plip, plap. The rain gets her soft and cool. But today the rain will not stop. Her nest is wet. Her feet are cold. She feels sad. "I want it dry," she says.

Faye sees a green light across a big field. It blinks in the early morning. Green light. She wants to go to the green light. "I can be dry there," she thinks. The grass is deep. She steps on a sharp branch. Ouch. Her foot hurts. She cannot walk. Now she is sad and stuck. She looks at the green light. Green light. Green light.

A big flag waves near her nest. It is red and warm. She hides under the flag. The flag keeps the rain off. A man comes. He sees her hurt foot. He puts a leaf on it. He is proud of his kind work. Faye is dry now. She peeks out. The green light is still far. Green light. She cannot reach it. But her foot is okay. She sits under the flag, warm and safe.

Little Faye the duck sat in the rain. The rain went tap, tap, tap on her head. She was sad.

Faye had a little problem. Her nest was wet. She wanted a dry place. She was proud of her nest. But now it was soggy.

Then she saw the green light. It was across a big field. The green light was far away. It was small and bright.

Faye forgot the rain. She forgot her wet nest. She only saw the green light. She wanted the green light.

She walked to the field. The rain got on her flag. She did not care. She just looked at the green light.

Tap, tap, tap went the rain. Faye did not hear it. She only thought, green light, green light, green light.

She walked and walked. The green light did not get closer. The field was too big.

Faye got cold. She got tired. She sat down in the mud. The green light stayed far away.

The rain stopped. The sun came up. But Faye still could not reach the green light. She was too small. It was too far.

Faye put her head down. She was sad. She never got the green light.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Carl gave Finn a rainstick for his birthday. It was long and brown. Little seeds clicked inside when Finn turned it. Finn loved that soft sound. He took it everywhere in his wagon. He said it sounded like rain.
 
One snowy day, Finn pulled his wagon up the hill. The town was white and quiet. He stopped to fix his hat. It was messy and falling down. Then he saw it. Far away, on a roof across the town, sat a green light. It was small and far. It did not click like rain. Finn wished he could reach it. But the snow was deep. His wagon was slow. He held his rainstick and made rain sounds instead.
 
Then the green light blinked. It was not a light at all. It was a cat with green eyes. The cat yawned and walked away.
 
Finn laughed. He turned his rainstick. The seeds clicked soft. Some lights are just cats. Some joy is right in your hands.

stories.name: Finn

stories.text:
Carefully, Finn shook the rainstick. It sounded like soft rain. He made it from a long tube and many tiny seeds. He liked the shush-shush sound.

Snow fell outside. Finn pulled his wagon to the window. He put the rainstick in it. The wagon was messy with toys.

Then Finn saw a small green light. It sat on a roof across the town. The green light was far away. It blinked in the snow.

Finn wanted to touch it. He tried to fix his wagon to go faster. But the wheels stuck in the snow. The green light stayed far.

He shook the rainstick again. Shush-shush. The green light seemed to listen. Finn smiled.

He looked down. His little sister was crying. She wanted the rainstick too.

Finn gave it to her. She stopped crying. She shook it. Shush-shush.

The green light blinked once more. Then snow covered it.

Finn did not need to reach it. He had the rain sound. He had his sister. Some lights stay far. But warm hands are close.

The moral is: you cannot hold every light, but you can hold what matters.

stories.name: Finn

stories.text: Cold snow fell on the town. Finn pulled his wagon to the shed. He would fix a rainstick. He made it from a long tube. He put in tiny beads and seeds. He turned it. It made a soft, messy sound, like rain. Finn liked it. He turned it again. Then he saw the green light. It was on a roof across the town. The snow made it glow. He turned the rainstick. He saw the green light. He walked to the window. He turned the rainstick. The green light did not move. He stood there a long time. He wanted to touch it. He could not. The beads in the stick slid down. It sounded like rain on a window. His little sister woke up. She was cold. She asked for a song. Finn gave her the rainstick. She shook it and smiled. The green light was still there. But now the small sound was here. He could hold it. The green light is far, but small joys are near. That is the true fix for a wanting heart.

stories.text:
Carefully Finn turned the rainstick. Tiny seeds slid down inside. They made a soft sound like rain. Finn loved that sound. He took the rainstick everywhere, even on his wagon.

Then Finn saw the green light. It sat on a roof across the town. The snow fell soft and white. The green light glowed through the snow. Finn wanted to touch it.

He pulled his wagon through the messy snow. He wanted to fix his eyes on the green light. The green light blinked far away.

At the corner, the green light was still far. Finn climbed a hill. The green light stayed small. He sat down in the snow. His wagon tipped over.

Finn looked down at his hands. The rainstick was gone. It had fallen in the messy snow. He felt sad. The green light did not care.

Then Finn heard a soft sound. It was rain. His rainstick was playing by itself in the snow. Finn laughed.

The green light is pretty, but the thing you hold can make its own music.

stories.name: Finn

features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Carl the rainstick made soft sounds when Finn turned it. It sounded like rain. Finn liked that. He pulled it in his wagon through the snow.

Then Finn saw the green light. It was on a roof across the town. The green light glowed in the white sky. Oh, the green light. He wanted the green light.

He tried to fix his wagon to go faster. The snow made it messy. He fell down. He got up. Green light. Green light. He could not stop thinking about the green light. Green light, green light, green light.

His mama called him home for soup. Finn did not want soup. He wanted the green light.

But then he shook the rainstick. It rained soft sounds on his hands. The green light was far away. The rain was right here.

The twist was this: the green light was just a kite stuck on a roof. It never rained there at all.

Some lights are pretty but far. The small sounds in your own hands are yours.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on a bridge over the river
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Pete the seal flipped in the river. Nate watched from the muddy bank. "Look, Dad! He wants my bread!"

"He wants to play," said Dad. "Not lunch."

Nate ran to the old bridge. He leaned way over. A small sailboat drifted by. Its sail was white and fat.

"Wait for me, Pete!" Nate called.

But Pete did not wait. The seal swam off. Nate frowned. His boat was stuck near the rocks. The little problem made him sad.

"Tiptoe on the planks," said Dad. "I'll pull the string."

Nate tiptoed. He tugged. The sailboat came free. Pete came back too. He splashed and barked.

Then Nate saw it. Far down the river, on a bridge, a green light blinked. It was small and far. He could not reach it. Not today.

"Time for lunch," said Dad.

Nate waved at the green light. "Bye, green light." He ate his bread. Pete got a tiny piece. The hot summer day felt just right.

stories.name: Nate

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Pete the seal swam up the river. Nate rowed his little sailboat after him. It was a hot summer day. "Wait, Pete!" Nate called. "Where are you going?" Pete did not stop.

Nate's boat got stuck in the muddy weeds. "Oh no," said Nate. He ate some bread and thought. Then he had an idea. He did a tiptoe dance on the deck. The boat rocked free.

Pete barked and flipped his tail. On the bridge over the river, Nate saw the green light. It blinked once, soft and far. He wished he could touch it. But Pete needed him. "Come back, Pete!" Nate laughed.

Then the green light shone again, low on the water. Nate rowed toward home. Pete followed close. The green light stayed behind them, small and bright. "Maybe tomorrow," Nate said. The green light did not answer.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on a bridge over the river
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Pete the seal flipped onto the warm dock. Nate sat beside him with a bag of bread. "We can share," Nate said. Pete clapped his flippers.

A sailboat drifted by. The wind was slow. Nate wanted to ride it. "Let's go," he said. But Pete could not climb the ladder. That was the problem.

So Nate pulled a rope. He made a little ramp. Pete slid up, muddy and happy. "You did it!" Nate laughed.

Then Nate saw the green light. It blinked on a bridge over the river. The green light was far away. He tiptoed to the boat's edge.

"Look," Nate whispered. The green light shone like a tiny star. Pete barked soft.

They sailed close. But the green light stayed far. Nate reached out. His hand caught only air.

"Some lights you just watch," Nate said. Pete nodded.

They ate bread as the sun went down. The green light kept glowing. Nate smiled anyway. The green light was not for touching. It was for seeing. And that was enough.

stories.name: Nate
